title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
嘉靖丙辰春二月復當會試
之期禮部尚書臣王用賓侍
郎臣吳山臣茅瓚以考試官
請
上命大學士臣李本學士臣尹臺
往莅其事而同考試則侍讀
===
臣瞿景淳臣陳陞侍講臣邢
一鳳中允臣董份修撰臣李
春芳臣唐汝楫臣陳謹編修
臣吳情臣呂調陽檢討臣裴
宇臣殷士儋都給事中臣王
鳴臣臣李敏給事中臣湯日
新署郎中臣方祥主事臣張

臣瞿〔景淳〕臣陳〔陞〕侍講臣邢

punctuated:
會試錄序

嘉靖丙辰春二月，復當會試之期，禮部尚書臣王用賓、侍郎臣吳山、臣茅瓚以考試官請。上命大學士臣李本、學士臣尹臺往莅其事。而同考試則侍讀臣瞿景淳、臣陳陞，侍講臣邢一鳳，中允臣董份，修撰臣李春芳、臣唐汝楫、臣陳謹，編修臣吳情、臣呂調陽，檢討臣裴宇、臣殷士儋，都給事中臣王鳴臣、臣李敏，給事中臣湯日新，署郎中臣方祥，主事臣張
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the second month of spring in the bingchen year of Jiajing (1556), the time for the Metropolitan Examination came round again. Your servants Wang Yongbin, Minister of Rites, and Wu Shan and Mao Zan, Vice Ministers, requested the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty commanded your servants Li Ben, Grand Secretary, and Yin Tai, Academician, to oversee the examination.

Serving as Associate Examiners were your servants Qu Jingchun and Chen Sheng, Readers-in-Waiting; Xing Yifeng, Expositor-in-Waiting; Dong Fen, Rectifier of the Heir Apparent; Li Chunfang, Tang Ruj i [Tang Ruji], and Chen Jin, Senior Compilers; Wu Qing and Lü Tiaoyang, Junior Compilers; Pei Yu and Yin Shidan, Examining Editors; Wang Mingchen and Li Min, Chief Supervising Secretaries; Tang Rixin, Supervising Secretary; Fang Xiang, Acting Bureau Director; and Zhang…, Secretary.

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
守直臣況叔祺監試則御史
臣徐紳臣吳遵暨內外執事
咸慎簡以充是月七日臣偕
諸臣既
陛辭臣本臣臺與知貢舉臣山
恭詣
迎和門稽首
===
辭伏蒙
皇上都賜湯飯夫校士
國朝重任而湯飯之
賜
聖恩優渥特出非常臣等榮幸感
激莫罄名言亦莫能報稱竊
念臣蒙
alt_text:
守直臣況〔叔祺〕監試則御史
臣徐〔紳〕臣吳〔遵〕暨內外執事
咸慎簡以充是月七日臣偕
諸臣既
陛辭臣本臣〔臺〕與知貢舉臣山
恭詣
迎和門稽首
===
辭伏蒙
皇上都賜湯飯夫校士
國朝重任而湯飯之
賜
聖恩優渥特出非常臣等榮幸感
激莫罄名言亦莫能報稱竊
念臣蒙
punctuated:
守直、臣況叔祺。監試則御史臣徐紳、臣吳遵，暨內外執事，咸慎簡以充。是月七日，臣偕諸臣既陛辭，臣本、臣臺與知貢舉臣山，恭詣迎和門，稽首辭，伏蒙皇上都賜湯飯。
夫校士，國朝重任，而湯飯之賜，聖恩優渥，特出非常。臣等榮幸感激，莫罄名言，亦莫能報稱。竊念臣蒙
translation_en:
…Shouzhi and your servant Kuang Shuqi. The examination monitors were the Censors, your servants Xu Shen and Wu Zun. They and the attendants serving inside and outside were all carefully selected to fill their posts. On the seventh day of this month, after I and the other officials had taken leave before the throne, your servants Ben and Tai, together with Shan, the official in charge of the examination, respectfully proceeded to Yinghe Gate and kowtowed in farewell. His Majesty graciously bestowed soup and rice upon us all.
Assessing scholars is a weighty responsibility in our dynasty. The bestowal of soup and rice was an exceptionally generous expression of imperial favor, far beyond the ordinary. We feel so honored and grateful that words cannot fully express it, nor can we adequately repay it. I humbly reflect that I have received…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
恩拔擢置諸
左右八年于兹涓埃未效今乃
得從是役附於以人事君之
後誠為幸矣仰惟我
皇上乾乾翼翼昭事
上帝三紀如一日凡民生之未遂
教化之未洽南北之未靖罔
===
不上廑
淵衷宵旰靡寧思得人以代天工
雖禹之籲俊湯之旁求文武
之克知灼見無以加焉前代
因事取士甚至設十科者今
乃盡取足於進士之一科於
此而不得人則無所得人矣
alt_text:
恩拔擢置諸
左右八年于茲涓埃未效今乃
得從是役附於以人事君之
後誠爲幸矣仰惟我
皇上乾乾翼翼昭事
上帝三紀如一日凡民生之未遂
教化之未洽南北之未靖罔
不上廑
===
淵衷宵旰靡寧思得人以代天工
雖禹之籲俊湯之旁求文武
之克知灼見無以加焉前代
因事取士甚至設十科者今
乃盡取足於進士之一科於
此而不得人則無所得人矣
punctuated: 恩拔擢，置諸左右，八年于兹，涓埃未效。今乃得從是役，附於以人事君之後，誠為幸矣。仰惟我皇上乾乾翼翼，昭事上帝，三紀如一日。凡民生之未遂、教化之未洽、南北之未靖，罔不上廑淵衷。宵旰靡寧，思得人以代天工，雖禹之籲俊、湯之旁求、文武之克知灼見，無以加焉。前代因事取士，甚至設十科者。今乃盡取足於進士之一科，於此而不得人，則無所得人矣。
translation_en: …graciously promoted and placed at Your Majesty’s side, I have now served for eight years without rendering even the slightest service. Now, however, I have been able to participate in this undertaking and join the ranks of those who serve their sovereign by finding worthy men. This is truly good fortune. I humbly reflect that our Emperor, ever diligent and reverent, has illustriously served the Lord on High for thirty-six years as steadfastly as for a single day. Wherever the people’s livelihood remains unfulfilled, moral instruction has yet to reach, or peace has yet to be secured in the north or south, these matters invariably weigh upon Your Majesty’s profound concern. Rising before dawn and eating late, without repose, Your Majesty seeks worthy men to carry out Heaven’s work. Even Yu’s summoning of outstanding men, Tang’s search far and wide, and Kings Wen and Wu’s discerning knowledge and clear insight could not surpass this. Earlier dynasties recruited men according to the tasks at hand, sometimes even establishing ten categories of selection. Now, however, all needs are met through the single category of metropolitan graduates (jinshi). If worthy men cannot be found through this channel, there is nowhere else to obtain them.

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
將何以仰副我
皇上任使至意臣不能無大懼也
既入院與諸臣胥誓戒曰在
外則防範之加嚴在内則鑒
别之必精惟慎惟公惟真才
之是得以承
休德圖報稱於萬一僉曰敢不同
===
心于時天下士就試者四千
四百有奇遵例三試之臣等
竭日夜之力遴選以俟
宸斷取三百人錄其名氏并其文
之純者二十篇以
獻臣等私相幸曰得是才也懼
其可少釋矣乎臣又撫卷而
alt_text:
將何以仰副我
皇上任使至意臣不能無大懼也
既入院與諸臣誓戒曰在
外則防範之加嚴在內則鑒
別之必精惟慎惟公惟真才
之是得以承
休德圖報稱於萬一僉曰敢不同
===
心于時天下士就試者四千
四百有奇遵例三試之臣等
竭日夜之力遴選以俟
宸斷取三百人錄其名氏并其文
之純者二十篇以
獻臣等私相幸曰得是才也懼
其可少釋矣乎臣又撫卷而
punctuated:
將何以仰副我皇上任使至意？臣不能無大懼也。既入院，與諸臣胥誓戒曰：「在外則防範之加嚴，在内則鑒别之必精。惟慎惟公，惟真才之是得，以承休德，圖報稱於萬一。」僉曰：「敢不同心！」
于時天下士就試者四千四百有奇。遵例三試之，臣等竭日夜之力，遴選以俟宸斷，取三百人，錄其名氏，并其文之純者二十篇以獻。臣等私相幸曰：「得是才也，懼其可少釋矣乎？」臣又撫卷而
translation_en:
How, then, could we fulfill His Majesty’s earnest intention to obtain men for service? Your servant could not but feel great apprehension. After entering the examination compound, I joined the other officials in a mutual pledge and admonition: “Outside, precautions must be made still stricter; inside, discrimination in judging must be exact. We must be cautious and impartial, seeking only men of true ability, so as to uphold His Majesty’s splendid virtue and endeavor to repay even a ten-thousandth of his favor.” All replied, “How could we dare not be of one mind!”
At that time, more than four thousand four hundred scholars from throughout the realm presented themselves for examination. Following precedent, we examined them in three sessions. We, your servants, worked to the utmost day and night, making selections to await His Majesty’s decision. Three hundred men were selected, and we recorded their names, together with twenty of their essays of the highest quality, for presentation to the throne. We privately congratulated one another, saying, “Having obtained men of such talent, may we now perhaps lay aside a little of our apprehension?” Then I again laid my hand upon the papers and…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
思之今之所取者文焉耳矣
由文言之經術精通記聞該
博辭語典麗議論暢達法律
練習籌畫詳當誠可舉之而
不疑即前代所稱十科取之
於是至足矣由是而華國而
任職而立事惟我
===
皇上所使如禹湯文武之得三俊
三宅豈特臣之懼可釋亦且
有餘榮哉雖然昔孔子卜而
不取于賁子貢曰夫賁亦好
矣何為不取乎孔子曰白而
白黑而黑夫賁何好乎蓋賁
文之謂也聖人所貴者純而
alt_text:
思之今之所取者文焉耳矣
由文言之經術精通記聞該
博辭語典麗議論暢達法律
練習籌畫詳當誠可舉之而
不疑即前代所稱十科取之
於是至足矣由是而華國而
任職而立事惟我
===
皇上所使如禹湯文武之得三俊
三宅豈特〔臣〕之懼可釋亦且
有餘榮哉雖然昔孔子卜而
不取于賁子貢曰夫賁亦好
矣何為不取乎孔子曰白而
白黑而黑夫賁何好乎蓋賁
文之謂也聖人所貴者純而
punctuated:
思之，今之所取者，文焉耳矣。由文言之，經術精通，記聞該博，辭語典麗，議論暢達，法律練習，籌畫詳當，誠可舉之而不疑。即前代所稱十科，取之於是，至足矣。由是而華國，而任職，而立事，惟我皇上所使。如禹湯文武之得三俊三宅，豈特臣之懼可釋，亦且有餘榮哉！
雖然，昔孔子卜而不取于賁。子貢曰：「夫賁亦好矣，何為不取乎？」孔子曰：「白而白，黑而黑，夫賁何好乎？」蓋賁，文之謂也。聖人所貴者純而
translation_en:
…reflect upon this: those whom we have now selected have been chosen solely for their writing. Judging from their writing, they possess thorough mastery of classical learning, extensive knowledge acquired through reading and listening, elegant and refined language, lucid and fluent argument, practiced familiarity with laws, and detailed and appropriate plans. Truly, we may recommend them without misgivings. Even measured against the so-called ten categories of selection of former ages, these men would amply suffice. Through these abilities they may bring distinction to the state, discharge official duties, and accomplish affairs, as Our Emperor employs them. As when Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu obtained outstanding men for the three principal offices, not only may your servant’s apprehension be relieved, but abundant honor may follow as well!
Nevertheless, Confucius once performed divination and declined to accept the hexagram Bi (Adornment). Zigong said, “Bi is surely good too. Why do you not accept it?” Confucius replied, “Let white be white and black be black. What is good about adornment?” Bi means embellishment. What the sage prized was purity…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
已是以取人必言行相顧表
裏如一始終無間如火之熱
如氷之寒如金石之堅剛抱
一以見於天下如白黒然夫
人皆知之而後為純也觀其
文則純而他日之所為或與
今日之文不相似口是而心
===
否面從而後言避難而趨易
假公而濟私見利而忘義若
背而馳駁亦甚矣奚取於文
之純哉語有之玉人之所患
患石之似玉者相劔之所患
患劔之似呉干者〔臣〕今執諸
士之文而决其為玉為呉干
alt_text:
已是以取人必言行相顧表
裏如一始終無間如火之熱
如氷之寒如金石之堅剛抱
一以見於天下如白黒然夫
人皆知之而後爲純也觀其
文則純而他日之所爲或與
今日之文不相似口是而心
===
否面從而後言避難而趨易
假公而濟私見利而忘義若
背而馳駁亦甚矣奚取於文
之純哉語有之玉人之所患
患石之似玉者相劒之所患
患劒之似吳干者臣今執諸
生之文而决其爲玉爲吳干
punctuated: 已。是以取人，必言行相顧，表裏如一，始終無間，如火之熱，如氷之寒，如金石之堅剛，抱一以見於天下，如白黒然，夫人皆知之，而後為純也。觀其文則純，而他日之所為，或與今日之文不相似，口是而心否，面從而後言，避難而趨易，假公而濟私，見利而忘義，若背而馳，駁亦甚矣，奚取於文之純哉？語有之：「玉人之所患，患石之似玉者；相劔之所患，患劔之似呉干者。」〔臣〕今執諸士之文，而决其為玉、為呉干
translation_en: …and nothing more. Thus, in selecting men, their words and deeds must accord, their outward conduct and inner character must be one, and they must remain consistent from beginning to end. Like the heat of fire, the cold of ice, and the hardness of metal and stone, they must hold fast to unity of purpose and manifest it before the world, as unmistakably as white and black. Only when everyone recognizes this may they be deemed pure. If their writings appear pure, but their subsequent actions fail to resemble what they write today—if their mouths assent while their hearts dissent, if they comply to one's face but speak against one afterward, avoid difficulty and seek ease, use public business to advance private interests, or forget righteousness at the sight of profit—then their conduct runs in the opposite direction, and their impurity is extreme. What value, then, is there in the purity of their writing? There is a saying: “What troubles a jade worker is stone that resembles jade; what troubles an appraiser of swords is a sword that resembles a famed Wu Gan blade.” Your servant now takes these candidates’ writings and judges them to be jade and Wu Gan blades…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
矣諸士果爲玉乎爲吳干乎
則純乎其純誠哉國之至寶
世之利器代天工以濟時艱
其效可佇而俟也否則孔子
之所謂貴者臣之懼方大耳
尚敢自幸耶書曰彰厥有常
吉哉易曰視履考祥其旋元
===
吉願諸士勗之
榮祿大夫太子太保禮部尚
書兼文淵閣大學士李本謹
序
alt_text:
矣諸士果爲玉乎爲兵乎乎
則純乎其純誠哉國之至寶
世之利器代天工以濟時艱
其效可佇而俟也否則亂孔子
之所謂貢者臣之懼方大耳
尚敢自幸耶書曰彰厥有常
吉哉易曰視履考祥其旋元
===
吉願諸士勗之
榮祿大夫太子太保禮部尚
書兼文淵閣大學士李本謹
序
punctuated:
矣。諸士果爲玉乎，爲吳干乎？則純乎其純，誠哉，國之至寶，世之利器！代天工以濟時艱，其效可佇而俟也。否則，孔子之所謂貴者，臣之懼方大耳，尚敢自幸耶？《書》曰：「彰厥有常，吉哉！」《易》曰：「視履考祥，其旋元吉。」願諸士勗之。
榮祿大夫、太子太保、禮部尚書兼文淵閣大學士李本謹序。
translation_en:
…indeed. Are these gentlemen truly jade, truly swords of Wu and Gan? Then, pure in their purity, they are indeed the nation's most precious treasures and the world's effective instruments! Acting on Heaven's behalf to relieve the difficulties of the age, they may soon be expected to show results. Otherwise, as regards what Confucius called “precious” [?], my apprehension as your servant would only grow greater. Would I still dare congratulate myself?
The Book of Documents says: “Manifest your constancy: auspicious indeed!” The Book of Changes says: “Examine your conduct and assess the auspicious signs; on its completion comes supreme good fortune.” May you gentlemen strive toward this.
Preface respectfully composed by Li Ben, Grand Master for Glorious Happiness, Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Rites, and concurrently Grand Secretary of the Wenyuan Hall.

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
嘉靖三十五年會試
知貢舉官
資善大夫太子少保禮部尚書兼翰林院學士王用賓〔允興陝西咸寧縣人辛丑進士〕
通議大夫禮部左侍郎兼翰林院侍讀學士吳山〔曰靜江西高安縣人乙未進士〕
考試官
榮祿大夫太子太保禮部尚書兼文淵閣大學士李本〔汝立浙江餘姚縣人壬辰進士〕
中憲大夫詹事府少詹事兼翰林院侍讀學士掌院事尹臺〔崇基江西永新縣人乙未進士〕
同考試官
翰林院侍讀瞿景淳〔師道直隸常熟縣人甲辰進士〕
===

翰林院侍講邢一鳳〔伯羽南京龍江左衛籍河南祥符縣人辛丑進士〕
右春坊右中允董份〔用均浙江烏程縣人辛丑進士〕
翰林院修撰儒林郎李春芳〔子實直隸興化縣籍句容縣人丁未進士〕
翰林院修撰儒林郎唐汝楫〔思濟浙江蘭谿縣人庚戌進士〕
翰林院修撰承務郎陳謹〔德言福建閩縣人癸丑進士〕

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Thirty-fifth Year of Jiajing (1556)

Directors of the Examination

Wang Yongbin, Grand Master for Assisting Goodness, Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent, and Minister of Rites concurrently serving as Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Yunxing; he was from Xianning County, Shaanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the xinchou year (1541).

Wu Shan, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites concurrently serving as Academician Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Yuejing; he was from Gao’an County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).

Examiners

Li Ben, Grand Master for Glorious Happiness, Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, and Minister of Rites concurrently serving as Grand Secretary of the Wenyuan Pavilion. His courtesy name was Ruli; he was from Yuyao County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the renchen year (1532).

Yin Tai, Grand Master for Exemplary Service and Junior Supervisor of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, concurrently serving as Academician Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and administering the Academy’s affairs. His courtesy name was Chongji; he was from Yongxin County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).

Associate Examiners

Qu Jingchun, Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Shidao; he was from Changshu County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiachen year (1544).

Chen Sheng, Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Jinfu; he was from Yuyao County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Xing Yifeng, Lecturer-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Boyu; he was registered in the Longjiang Left Guard at Nanjing, originated from Xiangfu County, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Dong Fen, Right Companion of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent. His courtesy name was Yongjun; he was from Wucheng County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Li Chunfang, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman of the Forest of Scholars. His courtesy name was Zishi; he was registered in Xinghua County, Zhili, originated from Jurong County, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Tang Ruji, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman of the Forest of Scholars. His courtesy name was Siji; he was from Lanxi County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the gengxu year (1550).

Chen Jin, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Undertaking Service. His courtesy name was Deyan; he was from Min County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Wu Qing, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman of the Forest of Literature. His courtesy name was Yizhong; he was from Wuxi County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiachen year (1544).

Lü Diaoyang, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman of the Forest of Literature. His courtesy name was Heqing; he was registered in the Guilin Central Guard, Guangxi, originated from Daye County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the gengxu year (1550).

Pei Yu, Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Attendant Service. His courtesy name was Zida; he was from Zezhou, Shanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Yin Shidan, courtesy name Zhengfu, was an Examining Editor in the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Exemplary Service. He was registered in Licheng County, Shandong, and was a native of Wuding Subprefecture; he became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in 1547.

Zhang Guochen, courtesy name Ruwen, was Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Revenue, with the rank of Gentleman for Service. He was from Taihe County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1544.

Li Min, courtesy name Chunfu, was Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Justice, with the rank of Gentleman for Service. He was from Yuci County, Shanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Tang Rixin, courtesy name Maozhao, was a Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Rites, with the rank of Gentleman for Attendant Service. He was from Xiushui County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1550.

Fang Xiang, courtesy name Lüxiang, was a Secretary serving as acting Director of the Bureau of Military Appointments in the Ministry of War, with the rank of Gentleman for Virtuous Conduct. He was from Fuliang County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Zhang Shouzhi, courtesy name Shiju, was a Secretary in the Bureau of Personnel in the Ministry of Personnel, with the rank of Gentleman for Virtuous Conduct. He was from Zunhua County, Shuntian Prefecture, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1544.

Kuang Shuqi, courtesy name Jifu, was a Secretary in the Sichuan Bureau of the Ministry of Justice, with the rank of Gentleman for Uprightness. He was from Gao’an County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1550.

Examination Monitoring Officials:

Xu Shen, courtesy name Sixing, was an Investigating Censor for the Jiangxi Circuit, with the rank of Gentleman for Scholarly Service. He was from Jiande County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1541.

Wu Zun, courtesy name Gonglu, was an Investigating Censor for the Henan Circuit, with the rank of Gentleman for Scholarly Service. He was from Haining County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Proctors:

Jia Heng, courtesy name Shouzhun, was a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, with the rank of Gentleman for Virtuous Conduct. He was from Shulu County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Wu Zhongli, courtesy name Dajie, was a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, with the rank of Gentleman for Uprightness. He was from Guichi County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Officials Responsible for Printing Examination Papers:

Liu Chaozuo, courtesy name Daoqing, was Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, with the rank of Grand Master for Counsel. He was from Anfu County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1544.

Song Tingbiao, courtesy name Jinzhi, was a Secretary serving as acting Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, with the rank of Gentleman for Virtuous Conduct. He was from Lingui County, Guangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Yang Boxiang, courtesy name Boxiang, was a Drafter in the Secretariat, with the rank of Gentleman for Exemplary Service. He was registered in Dantu County, Zhili, and was a native of Taihe Subprefecture, Yunnan; he held student status by virtue of an official’s privilege (guansheng).

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

臣事君以忠。
詩云：「維天之命，於穆不已！」蓋曰天之所以為天也。
大而化之之謂聖，聖而不可知之之謂神。

易

剛健篤實輝光，日新其德。
中孚以利貞，乃應乎天也。
盛德大業至矣哉！富有之謂大業，日新之謂盛德。
神也者，妙萬物而為言者也。

書

至誠感神，矧茲有苗！禹拜昌言，曰：「俞！」班師振旅。帝乃誕敷文德，舞干羽于兩階。
惟箘簵楛，三邦厎貢厥名，包匭菁茅。
丕若有夏歷年，式勿替有殷歷年。
奉答天命，和恒四方民，居師。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

A minister serves his ruler with loyalty.

The Book of Odes says: “Heaven’s mandate—oh, how profound and unceasing!” This speaks of what makes Heaven Heaven.

One who is great and transforms others is called a sage; a sage whose workings cannot be fathomed is called numinous.

Book of Changes

Firm and vigorous, substantial and solid, radiant and bright: he daily renews his virtue.

Inner Sincerity brings benefit through steadfast correctness; thus it accords with Heaven.

How consummate are abundant virtue and great achievement! Rich possession is called great achievement; daily renewal is called abundant virtue.

The numinous refers to the wondrous workings within the myriad things.

Book of Documents

Utmost sincerity moves the spirits—how much more these people of Youmiao! Yu bowed at these excellent words and said, “Yes!” He withdrew his army and put his troops in order. The emperor then spread the influence of civil virtue far and wide, and dancers bearing shields and feather plumes performed between the two stairways.

As for jun and lu bamboo and ku wood, the three states presented their tribute, “its names” [?]; fine mao grass was wrapped and placed in containers.

Greatly emulate the length of years enjoyed by the Xia; do not let the years of the Yin be cut short.

Reverently respond to Heaven’s mandate, bring harmony and constancy to the people of the four quarters, and settle the multitudes.

translation_en:
Book of Odes

The four stallions are very sturdy; the six reins are in hand. The dappled and bay horses are the central pair; the dun and black horses are the outer pair. Where the dragon-decorated shields meet are white-metal fittings, with buckles for the inner reins.

May the lord live ten thousand years and safeguard his household and state.

The phoenixes call upon that high ridge. The wutong trees grow on its sun-facing slope. Luxuriant and abundant is their foliage; harmonious and clear are the birds’ calls.

Day and night he laid the foundations of the mandate, profound and circumspect. Ah, continuing in luminous virtue, he devoted his whole heart.

Spring and Autumn Annals

In autumn, in the seventh month, on the gengwu day, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Qi, and the Marquis of Wei made a covenant at Wawu. Eighth year of Duke Yin.

In summer, the Marquis of Qi and the Marquis of Wei exchanged pledges at Pu. Third year of Duke Huan.

The duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, Guang, heir apparent of Qi, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, and the Viscount of Xiao Zhu in attacking Zheng; they assembled at Xiaoyu. Eleventh year of Duke Xiang.

The men of Qi attacked the Mountain Rong. Thirtieth year of Duke Zhuang. In the sixth month, the Marquis of Qi came to present the spoils of victory over the Rong. Thirty-first year of Duke Zhuang.

Qu Wan of Chu came to make a covenant with the army; the covenant was concluded at Shaoling. Fourth year of Duke Xi.

Jisun Si and Zhongsun Heji led an army to demolish the fortifications of Fei. Twelfth year of Duke Ding.

Book of Rites

德教所推行威刑所振遏及夫禮制之裁定
紀綱之修飭自
登極以迄于今
綸言昭示爛然與日月同光矣盖我
二祖締造之功
皇上繼紹之烈敷揚翔洽譬風之噓拂萬類疾

===

夫鏡往古之迹欲以明當世之務也矧

以期奮熈於有待豈所以為士耶願敬

punctuated:
皇上神聖中興，作述兼隆，考諸三代而斟酌損益其未備。一時德教所推行，威刑所振遏，及夫禮制之裁定、紀綱之修飭，自登極以迄于今，綸言昭示，爛然與日月同光矣。盖我二祖締造之功、皇上繼紹之烈，敷揚翔洽，譬風之噓拂萬類，疾行而善入，薄海內外，幽遐無弗達者也。諸士誦服之久，亦嘗仰思而得其概乎？夫鏡往古之迹，欲以明當世之務也。矧茲聖謨洋洋，一代之大政出焉。諸士不詳繹其義，以期奮熈於有待，豈所以為士耶？願敬著于篇，以觀平居所學之大。

問：國家取材，首重明經之士。夫儒者窮經，本為致用計也。然三代而上，未聞有窮經之名，乃士之用世者，功烈非後世可
translation_en:
…His Majesty, in his divine sagacity, has brought about a restoration, excelling alike in creating institutions and carrying forward those inherited. He has examined the institutions of the Three Dynasties, weighing what to subtract or add to remedy their deficiencies. The propagation of moral instruction, the deterrent force of awe-inspiring punishments, the determination of ritual institutions, and the ordering of governing principles and discipline—all these, from his accession down to the present, have been clearly proclaimed in imperial pronouncements, shining as brilliantly as the sun and moon. The founding achievements of our two ancestral emperors and His Majesty’s glorious continuation of their work have thus been widely proclaimed and have spread everywhere. Like the wind breathing upon the myriad things, moving swiftly and penetrating readily, they reach every hidden and distant place throughout the lands within and beyond the seas.

You gentlemen have long recited and reverently embraced these pronouncements. Have you also reflected upon them with reverence and grasped their general purport? We take the deeds of antiquity as a mirror in order to understand the affairs of our own age. How much more does this apply to these abundant sagely counsels, from which issue the great policies of this dynasty! If you gentlemen do not carefully unfold their meaning, hoping to exert yourselves in advancing good government when the occasion awaits you, how can you fulfill your calling as scholars? Set this forth reverently in writing, so that we may observe the breadth of the learning you have cultivated in ordinary life.

Question: In selecting men of talent, the state places foremost those who understand the classics. Confucian scholars thoroughly investigate the classics with practical application as their fundamental aim. Yet in the Three Dynasties and earlier, the term “thorough investigation of the classics” was unheard of; nevertheless, the achievements of scholars who served the world were such that later ages could not…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
及不知何所學而能然歟漢表章六經
而經術始盛當時學者各守其經宜利
於用矣而考諸傳記則有未盡然者焉
分卦直日者或昧于保身說詩解頤者
終陷于阿附能明皇極之旨而志汙青
紫三獻賢良之策而學溺災異不知於
經何如也之數子者皆師授名家尚無
救乎其失餘可推而知巳豈經固不足
以適用抑其所以窮之者未盡歟唐雖
===
以明經取士而經術遠不逮漢疏義之
舛雜君子有遺譏焉迨宋真儒輩出師
徒日相講授六經傳註粲然明備於世
學者不惑所從嚮其明經之學亦有與
漢儒同者歟使竟其用不知可幾於三
代之士否乎諸士通經以待用其必有
定見也願聞其說
問班固氏志藝文刪劉氏七畧以備篇籍
使後世博聞之士有考焉其志亦勤矣

punctuated:
及，不知何所學而能然歟？漢表章六經，而經術始盛。當時學者各守其經，宜利於用矣，而考諸傳記，則有未盡然者焉。分卦直日者或昧于保身，說詩解頤者終陷于阿附；能明皇極之旨而志汙青紫，三獻賢良之策而學溺災異，不知於經何如也？之數子者皆師授名家，尚無救乎其失，餘可推而知巳。豈經固不足以適用，抑其所以窮之者未盡歟？唐雖以明經取士，而經術遠不逮漢，疏義之舛雜，君子有遺譏焉。迨宋真儒輩出，師徒日相講授，六經傳註粲然明備於世，學者不惑所從嚮。其明經之學亦有與漢儒同者歟？使竟其用，不知可幾於三代之士否乎？諸士通經以待用，其必有定見也，願聞其說。
問：班固氏志藝文，刪劉氏七畧以備篇籍，使後世博聞之士有考焉，其志亦勤矣。
translation_en:
…match. What, one wonders, did they study that enabled them to achieve this? Under the Han, the Six Classics were publicly honored, and classical learning began to flourish. Scholars of that time each devoted themselves to their own classic, which ought to have served them well in practice. Yet examination of the historical accounts and biographies shows that this was not entirely so. One who assigned hexagrams to preside over particular days nevertheless failed to understand how to preserve himself; one whose explanations of the Odes brought smiles to his listeners ultimately fell into obsequious dependence. One could elucidate the meaning of the August Norm, yet sullied his aspirations by pursuing the blue and purple insignia of office; another submitted policy essays three times in the examination for the Worthy and Good, yet his learning became mired in calamities and anomalies. How, one wonders, did they stand in relation to the Classics? These men were all renowned scholars who had received instruction from masters, yet even this could not remedy their failings. The rest may be inferred. Are the Classics inherently inadequate for practical use, or did these scholars fail to investigate them fully?
Although the Tang recruited officials through the examination in elucidating the Classics, its classical learning fell far short of that of the Han. Gentlemen left criticisms of the errors and inconsistencies in its subcommentaries. By the Song, true Confucian scholars emerged in succession. Masters and disciples lectured and instructed one another daily, and commentaries and annotations on the Six Classics became splendidly clear and complete, available to the world. Students were no longer uncertain where to turn. Did their learning in elucidating the Classics nevertheless share anything with that of the Han scholars? Had they been able to put their learning fully into practice, could they have approached the scholars of the Three Dynasties? You gentlemen have mastered the Classics while awaiting employment and must surely have settled views. We wish to hear your explanations.
Question: In compiling his Treatise on Literature, Ban Gu abridged Liu’s Seven Summaries (Qi lüe) to provide a comprehensive record of writings, giving broadly learned scholars of later generations something to consult. His endeavor was indeed diligent.

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
然其舛謬不中於理者蓋多試與諸士
論之固所志凡十家各列所從出之官
以為其要歸亦六經之支裔也取其長可
通萬方之畧似矣然其所稱十官者諸
家之書果皆由之以出乎否也夫既曰
十家矣而又曰可觀者九家不知孰在
其所遺耶藝文莫先於六藝儒不列六
藝而類於九家儒非學聖人者乎抑為
儒者不足與於六藝也儒於道為最高
===
取秦漢棼雜之書儕而殽之豈儒之術
無異於百家也固之識已陋矣後之襲
固以立議者多至不可勝紀夫才幾王
佐而學或溺於申韓道尊孔氏而智不
辨乎儒墨他若稱蘇張之辯有濟於諫
諍謂莊周之書知推尊乎聖人此又其
取舍不倫之大者其可以為訓乎夫學
者考信六藝故載籍雖博不當忘所决
擇也諸士必究意於是矣願一聞折衷

punctuated: 然其舛謬不中於理者蓋多，試與諸士論之。固所志凡十家，各列所從出之官，以為其要歸亦六經之支裔也，取其長可通萬方之畧，似矣。然其所稱十官者，諸家之書果皆由之以出乎？否也？夫既曰十家矣，而又曰可觀者九家，不知孰在其所遺耶？藝文莫先於六藝，儒不列六藝而類於九家，儒非學聖人者乎？抑為儒者不足與於六藝也？儒於道為最高，取秦漢棼雜之書儕而殽之，豈儒之術無異於百家也？固之識已陋矣，後之襲固以立議者多至不可勝紀。夫才幾王佐而學或溺於申韓，道尊孔氏而智不辨乎儒墨，他若稱蘇張之辯有濟於諫諍，謂莊周之書知推尊乎聖人，此又其取舍不倫之大者，其可以為訓乎？夫學者考信六藝，故載籍雖博，不當忘所决擇也。諸士必究意於是矣，願一聞折衷
translation_en: … Yet many of its errors and inconsistencies fail to accord with principle. Let us discuss these with you candidates. Ban Gu recorded ten schools in all, listing for each the office from which it originated. He considered their essential purport to derive from the Six Classics, and held that, by drawing on their strengths, one could comprehend methods for dealing with every circumstance. This seems plausible. Yet did the writings of these schools really all originate in the ten offices he named, or did they not? Having spoken of ten schools, he then says that nine are worthy of consideration. Which did he leave out? In the realm of writings and learning, nothing takes precedence over the Six Arts [the Six Classics]. Yet he places the Confucians among the nine schools rather than under the Six Arts. Are Confucians not students of the sages? Or are they unworthy of inclusion under the Six Arts? Confucian learning stands highest in relation to the Way. If one takes the miscellaneous writings of the Qin and Han and ranks them alongside it, mingling them together, does this mean that Confucian teaching is no different from that of the Hundred Schools? Ban Gu’s understanding was already shallow; those who subsequently followed him in formulating their arguments are too numerous to count. Some possessed talents approaching those of an adviser to a true king, yet their learning became immersed in the teachings of Shen Buhai and Han Fei; others honored Confucius in their teachings, yet lacked the discernment to distinguish Confucianism from Mohism. Other examples include praising the eloquence of Su Qin and Zhang Yi as useful for remonstrance, or claiming that the writings of Zhuang Zhou show an understanding of how to exalt the sages. These are still graver instances of indiscriminate acceptance and rejection. Can they serve as models? Scholars examine what is trustworthy by reference to the Six Arts. Thus, however extensive the written record, they must not forget the need to discriminate and choose. You candidates must surely have considered this deeply. We should like to hear your considered judgment …

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
之論
問兵制財賦國之大計歷代沿革載在史
冊者可稽也三代遠矣試以唐宋言之
唐初以府衞治兵張說變之而不善宋
之聚兵最冗王安石變為保甲而兵制
益不善豈安石固未足以知制兵之意
歟唐初以租庸調治財楊炎變之而不
善君子猶謂為一時之權者宋之糜財
最多安石變為條例而經制益不善豈
===
安石固不足以知治財賦之道歟其在

而紛更者猶得以藉口歟如光之謀則

alt_text:
之論
問兵制財賦國之大計歷代沿革載在史
冊者可稽也三代遠矣試以唐宋言之
唐初以府衛治兵張說變之而不善宋
之聚兵最冗王安石變為保甲而兵制
益不善豈安石固未足以知制兵之意
歟唐初以租庸調治財楊炎變之而不
善君子猶謂為一時之權者宋之糜財
最多安石變為條例而經制益不善豈
===
安石固不足以知治財賦之道歟其在
唐諸臣李泌嘗思復府兵矣陸贄嘗思
復租庸調矣而議不果行豈行之有本
末而復之果難歟始謀不審孰任其咎
歟其在宋若司馬光嘗放免保甲蠲除
條例矣而不久復行豈其事不可盡非
而紛更者猶得以藉口歟如光之謀則
宋之兵冗財匱又將何以救之歟夫兵
制財賦事自相須而唐宋興衰之幾在
punctuated:
之論。
問：兵制、財賦，國之大計，歷代沿革載在史冊者可稽也。三代遠矣，試以唐宋言之。唐初以府衞治兵，張說變之而不善；宋之聚兵最冗，王安石變為保甲，而兵制益不善。豈安石固未足以知制兵之意歟？唐初以租庸調治財，楊炎變之而不善，君子猶謂為一時之權者。宋之糜財最多，安石變為條例，而經制益不善。豈安石固不足以知治財賦之道歟？其在唐，諸臣李泌嘗思復府兵矣，陸贄嘗思復租庸調矣，而議不果行。豈行之有本末，而復之果難歟？始謀不審，孰任其咎歟？其在宋，若司馬光嘗放免保甲、蠲除條例矣，而不久復行。豈其事不可盡非，而紛更者猶得以藉口歟？如光之謀，則宋之兵冗財匱，又將何以救之歟？夫兵制、財賦，事固相須，而唐宋興衰之幾在
translation_en:
…a considered judgment on the matter.

Question: Military organization and fiscal administration are great affairs of state. Their changes through successive dynasties can be examined in the historical records. The Three Dynasties are remote; let us discuss the Tang and Song instead. At the beginning of the Tang, troops were organized through the garrison militia and guards. Zhang Yue changed this system, with poor results. The Song amassed an excessively large army; Wang Anshi changed the system to the baojia system of mutual-responsibility households, but military organization deteriorated further. Was Anshi fundamentally unable to understand the principles of organizing an army? At the beginning of the Tang, finances were administered through the grain tax, labor service or its commutation, and textile levy—the zu-yong-diao system. Yang Yan changed it, with poor results, yet gentlemen still called it an expedient suited to its time. The Song's expenditure was exceptionally wasteful. Anshi introduced new fiscal regulations, but fiscal administration deteriorated further. Was Anshi fundamentally unable to understand the proper way to administer revenues?

Among Tang ministers, Li Mi once contemplated restoring the garrison militia, and Lu Zhi once contemplated restoring the zu-yong-diao system, but their proposals were never implemented. Was this because implementation required attention to fundamentals and details, making restoration genuinely difficult? If the initial planning was insufficiently considered, who should bear the blame? In the Song, Sima Guang released households from baojia obligations and abolished the fiscal regulations, but these were soon reinstated. Was this because those measures could not be condemned in their entirety, so that advocates of repeated changes could still find a pretext? If Guang's proposals were followed, how else could the Song's excessive military establishment and depleted finances have been remedied? Military organization and fiscal administration are indeed mutually dependent, and the pivotal factors in the rise and decline of the Tang and Song lie in…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
此則法之變不變所繫不亦重耶諸士
即當其任宜如何而後可
問蠻夷有苗載自虞書淮夷玁狁見于周
雅盖夷狄之患聖世所不能免在制馭
之得其道耳今西北諸邊虜間入犯旋
即驅逐未有踰旬日者頃倭夷肆擾東
南乃累歲而未平
聖天子明見萬里之外易將徵師雖嘗奏績然
而羽檄之報未已也豈蕞爾之夷反强
===
於北虜耶抑遠近勢異而難易不同耶
自倭患始作謀議之臣覩時陳畧慷慨
之士懷憤獻忠其說亦多矣或曰莫急
于將或曰責在守令或曰兵少或曰財
乏或曰莫相救援或曰人不能固守或
曰海防所最先者其說孰為要歟或又

皇祖時倭已發難嘗遣重臣修築海上諸城備
禦之道甚密茲可舉而行之歟夫說多

punctuated:
此，則法之變不變所繫不亦重耶？諸士即當其任，宜如何而後可？
問：蠻夷有苗，載自虞書；淮夷玁狁，見于周雅。盖夷狄之患，聖世所不能免，在制馭之得其道耳。今西北諸邊，虜間入犯，旋即驅逐，未有踰旬日者。頃倭夷肆擾東南，乃累歲而未平。聖天子明見萬里之外，易將徵師，雖嘗奏績，然而羽檄之報未已也。豈蕞爾之夷反强於北虜耶？抑遠近勢異而難易不同耶？自倭患始作，謀議之臣覩時陳畧，慷慨之士懷憤獻忠，其說亦多矣。或曰莫急于將，或曰責在守令，或曰兵少，或曰財乏，或曰莫相救援，或曰人不能固守，或曰海防所最先者。其說孰為要歟？或又言，自皇祖時，倭已發難，嘗遣重臣修築海上諸城，備禦之道甚密，茲可舉而行之歟？夫說多
translation_en:
…on this, then, does not the decision whether or not to change institutions carry great consequences? If you gentlemen were to assume responsibility for these matters, how should you proceed to achieve a satisfactory result?
Question: The Man and Yi peoples and the Miao are recorded as early as the Documents of Yu; the Huaiyi and Xianyun appear in the Zhou Odes. Even an age of sage rule cannot avoid troubles from the non-Chinese peoples: what matters is finding the proper way to control them. At present, raiders occasionally invade the various northwestern frontiers, but they are promptly driven out; none has remained longer than ten days. Recently, however, Japanese raiders have ravaged the southeast, and several years have passed without their being subdued. The sagely Son of Heaven clearly perceives affairs ten thousand li away and has replaced commanders and summoned troops. Although successes have been reported, urgent military dispatches continue to arrive. Can these petty barbarians actually be stronger than the northern raiders? Or do differences in circumstances between nearby and distant regions make one easier to deal with than the other?
Since the Japanese troubles began, ministers engaged in deliberation have assessed the times and presented strategies, while impassioned men, filled with indignation, have offered their loyal counsel. Their proposals have been numerous. Some say that nothing is more urgent than choosing commanders; some that responsibility rests with prefects and magistrates; some that troops are too few; some that funds are lacking; some that forces fail to come to one another’s aid; some that the people cannot hold their positions securely; and some that coastal defense must take first priority. Which of these arguments addresses the essential point? Others say that the Japanese had already begun causing trouble in the time of the imperial ancestor, who dispatched senior ministers to build and repair the coastal cities’ fortifications, making very thorough arrangements for defense. Can these measures now be taken up and put into practice? When proposals are numerous…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
則計易摇計失則功難成當事者所以
屢動而輒舛也今倭患雖急于東南而
調兵輸餉天下莫不繹騷者諸士必隱
於中久矣出乎羣策之外有至計可裨
廟算者其為我悉陳之
alt_text:
則計易採計失則功難成當事者所以
屢動而輒舛也今倭患雖急于東南而
調兵輸餉天下莫不繹騷者諸士必隱
於中久矣出乎羣策之外有至計可禆
廟算者其爲我悉陳之
punctuated: 則計易摇，計失則功難成，當事者所以屢動而輒舛也。今倭患雖急于東南，而調兵輸餉，天下莫不繹騷者，諸士必隱於中久矣。出乎羣策之外，有至計可裨廟算者，其為我悉陳之。
translation_en: …then plans are easily unsettled; when planning goes awry, success is difficult to achieve. This is why those responsible repeatedly take action yet invariably go wrong. Although the threat from the wokou raiders is now most pressing in the southeast, the mobilization of troops and transport of provisions have thrown the entire realm into turmoil. You gentlemen must long have felt anguish over this in your hearts. If, beyond all the proposals already offered, you have an excellent plan that could assist the court’s deliberations, set it forth for me in full.

諸大綬

之義可以觀所養宜錄以式
同考試官編修呂批講忠字親切懇到讀
之可識為臣之義
同考試官修撰唐批人臣事君之義此作
===
得之而詞復精實可以式矣
同考試官右中允董批言簡而當忠愛真切
可以知其衷矣錄之
考試官侍講學士尹批發得人臣事君之心出可錄
考試官大學士李批意精辭達
聖人發事君之義而臣道盡之矣盖忠者事君
之義也欲為臣盡臣道舍忠何以哉聖人之意
若謂天下之不可易者分也夫人之所當自盡
者心也是故民生於三而事君為大則思委質

同考試官編修呂批：講忠字親切懇到，讀之可識為臣之義。
同考試官修撰唐批：人臣事君之義，此作得之，而詞復精實，可以式矣。
同考試官右中允董批：言簡而當，忠愛真切，可以知其衷矣，錄之。
考試官侍講學士尹批：發得人臣事君之心出，可錄。
考試官大學士李批：意精辭達。

聖人發事君之義，而臣道盡之矣。盖忠者，事君之義也。欲為臣盡臣道，舍忠何以哉？聖人之意若謂：天下之不可易者，分也；夫人之所當自盡者，心也。是故民生於三，而事君為大，則思委質
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“A minister serves his ruler with loyalty.”
Zhu Dashou

Comment by Associate Examiner Fang, Acting Director: Without wasting words, this fully explores the meaning of loyalty to the ruler. It reveals the author's self-cultivation and should be selected as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Lü, Compiler: The explanation of the word “loyalty” is apposite, earnest, and thorough. Reading it, one can understand the duty of a minister.

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Senior Compiler: This composition grasps the duty of a minister in serving his ruler, and its language is also refined and substantial. It can serve as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Dong, Right Assistant Instructor: The language is concise and apt; its loyalty and affection are sincere and deeply felt. From it one can know the author's inner heart. Select it.

Comment by Examiner Yin, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: It brings out the heart with which a minister serves his ruler. It merits selection.

Comment by Examiner Li, Grand Secretary: The ideas are refined, and the language conveys them effectively.

The Sage elucidated the duty of serving one's ruler, and therein the way of the minister is fully expressed. For loyalty is the duty owed in serving one's ruler. If one wishes, as a minister, to fulfill the minister's way, how could one do so apart from loyalty? The Sage's meaning seems to be this: what cannot be altered in the world is one's allotted station; what each person ought to give to the utmost is his heart. Thus, since the people owe their lives to three sources, and serving the ruler is of greatest importance, one must think of pledging oneself to his service…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
以盡天下之大倫達道有五而惟君為尊則點
竭忠以行天下之大義有大臣焉有小臣焉職
雖不同均之熙帝載也必因其所任以殫精白
之誠有近臣焉有遠臣焉地雖或異均之從王
事也必隨其所在以堅勿欺之志慶遭逢之盛
凡可以匡濟者無不為也勵匪懈於夙夜蓋公
爾忘私矣感知遇之隆凡可以圖報者無不至
也秉一節於始終蓋國爾忘家矣是知由君而
有臣之名由臣而有忠之道不忠不可以為臣
===
矣故曰臣事君以忠抑論中心為忠忠之義也
故事必由中者始可以言忠然則人臣之事君
凡苟且矯飾至于一事之小一念之微少有不
出於中心者皆不忠之類也必充此之義以致
於極而後可
詩云維天之命於穆不已蓋曰天之所以
為天也
金達

以盡天下之大倫。達道有五，而惟君為尊，則點竭忠以行天下之大義。有大臣焉，有小臣焉，職雖不同，均之熙帝載也，必因其所任以殫精白之誠。有近臣焉，有遠臣焉，地雖或異，均之從王事也，必隨其所在以堅勿欺之志。慶遭逢之盛，凡可以匡濟者無不為也，勵匪懈於夙夜，蓋公爾忘私矣；感知遇之隆，凡可以圖報者無不至也，秉一節於始終，蓋國爾忘家矣。是知由君而有臣之名，由臣而有忠之道，不忠不可以為臣矣。故曰：「臣事君以忠。」抑論中心為忠，忠之義也。故事必由中者，始可以言忠。然則人臣之事君，凡苟且矯飾，至于一事之小、一念之微，少有不出於中心者，皆不忠之類也。必充此之義以致於極，而後可。
詩云：「維天之命，於穆不已！」蓋曰天之所以為天也。
金達
同考試官中書批〔所以為天處最難發〕
translation_en:
…to fulfill the great human relationship under Heaven. There are five universally binding relationships, and the ruler alone holds the most honored position; thus one must [?] exhaust one’s loyalty to practice the great righteousness under Heaven. There are high ministers and lesser ministers: although their offices differ, all alike further the sovereign’s undertakings. Each must therefore devote the utmost purity and sincerity to the responsibilities entrusted to him. There are ministers near the ruler and ministers far away: although their locations may differ, all alike serve the king’s affairs. Wherever they are, they must hold firmly to the resolve never to deceive him. Rejoicing in the good fortune of serving in such flourishing times, they leave nothing undone that might assist and sustain the realm. Diligent and unremitting morning and night, they forget private interests in their devotion to public duty. Moved by the ruler’s generous recognition and favor, they spare no effort to repay him. Maintaining unwavering integrity from beginning to end, they forget their families in their devotion to the state. Thus we know that it is through the ruler that one bears the name of minister, and through being a minister that one has the way of loyalty to follow. Without loyalty, one cannot be a minister. Hence the saying: “A minister serves his ruler with loyalty.”
Moreover, to speak of loyalty as what is within the heart is to explain its meaning. Only when service proceeds from within can it be called loyal. Thus, in a minister’s service to his ruler, all careless expediency and false embellishment—even in the smallest affair or the faintest thought—belong to the category of disloyalty if they depart in the slightest from what is truly in his heart. Only by extending this principle to its utmost limit can one serve as one should.
The Book of Odes says: “The mandate of Heaven—ah, how profound and unceasing!” This speaks of that by which Heaven is Heaven.
Jin Da
Comment by the Associate Examiner, a Secretariat Drafter: 〔The point concerning that by which Heaven is Heaven is the most difficult to expound…〕

…to elucidate. This composition strips away empty phrasing, while its reasoning is precise and thorough. It may serve as a model.
Associate Examiner Pei, Examining Editor, comments: It grasps the meaning of utmost sincerity operating without cease; it is no mere display of rhetoric. It should be selected as a model.
Associate Examiner Xing, Expositor, comments: Its language is concise and its reasoning clear. It grasps the poet’s intent in speaking of Heaven. This is a fine scholar, fully deserving of a strong recommendation.
Associate Examiner Chen, Reader, comments: It elucidates almost exhaustively what makes Heaven Heaven. The writer evidently understands the Way of Heaven profoundly. Select it.

The Doctrine of the Mean quotes the Book of Poetry to explain the subtle workings of the Way of Heaven: these are entirely the operation of utmost sincerity. Sincerity is the Way of Heaven. By observing the ceaselessness of Heaven’s Way, one can understand the sincerity of the sage. Zisi’s meaning is presumably that the way of utmost sincerity originates in Heaven. To speak of Heaven without knowing that Heaven’s mandate is unceasing is not to know Heaven. The Book of Poetry says: “The mandate of Heaven—ah, how profound and unceasing!” Heaven is vast and great; yet the poet singles out the ceaselessness of its mandate because he is speaking of what makes Heaven Heaven. Its patterns and images are arrayed in profusion, yet there must be something that controls their animating mechanism; its transformations flow onward, yet there must be something that makes their functioning wondrous. What establishes the Way of Heaven is its mandate; what makes that mandate unceasing is sincerity. Yin and yang succeed each other, from antiquity to the present, without pausing for a single breath. text:

一息之間則悠久者得之以有常而四時由是

則運乎沖漠而無端焉自散殊之形求之天也
而所以爲天者則行乎渾淪而不止焉是則天

窮，而萬物囿此覆幬矣。動靜相乘，貫終始而無一息之間，則悠久者得之以有常，而四時由是錯行矣。自造化之迹觀之，天也，而所以爲天者，則運乎沖漠而無端焉；自散殊之形求之，天也，而所以爲天者，則行乎渾淪而不止焉。是則天道不已，聖人之道亦不已。觀乎天，則見聖人，不其然哉？雖然，天地以誠而成化，聖人以誠而弘功業，其道一也。至於天地之所不能者，匪聖人成能，則造化有時而窮。財成輔相之道，聖人有不得而辭其任者矣。故曰：「至誠賛天地之化育。」
大而化之之謂聖，聖而不可知之之謂神。
馮謙

translation_en:
…without limit, and the myriad things are encompassed beneath this covering. Activity and stillness succeed one another, extending from end to beginning without a moment’s interruption; thus Heaven’s enduring nature attains constancy through it, and the four seasons proceed in alternation. Viewed through the traces of creation and transformation, it is Heaven; yet that which makes it Heaven operates in empty stillness, without beginning. Sought through the forms of distinct and diverse things, it is Heaven; yet that which makes it Heaven moves within undifferentiated unity, without ceasing. Thus Heaven’s Way never ceases, and the sage’s Way likewise never ceases. By observing Heaven, one sees the sage—is this not so? Nevertheless, Heaven and Earth accomplish transformation through sincerity, and the sage enlarges his achievements through sincerity: their Way is one. As for what Heaven and Earth cannot accomplish, unless the sage brings their capacities to fulfillment, creation and transformation will sometimes reach their limits. In shaping and completing their workings and assisting them, the sage bears a responsibility he cannot decline. Hence it is said: “Utmost sincerity assists the transforming and nourishing work of Heaven and Earth.”
“To be great and to transform is called sagehood; to be a sage and yet be beyond comprehension is called spiritual power.”
Feng Qian
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Chief Supervising Secretary: “The two terms ‘spiritual power’ and ‘sagehood’ are most difficult to grasp fully. In this composition, the language is seamlessly integrated, and the meaning becomes clear of itself. This, indeed, is writing of the highest order.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Chief Supervising Secretary: “Where it explains sagehood and spiritual power, the language is economical and the reasoning precise and apt. It may serve as a model.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Compiler: “Sagehood and spiritual power are simply the full realization of a single principle. This composition grasps that and elucidates it thoroughly. Its author seems to have devoted serious thought to the single thread that runs through all.”

Associate Examiner Li, Senior Compiler, comments: “Spirituality and sagehood are not easily described. Only in this piece have I seen language so refined and profound. Include it.”

The great worthy explains why sagehood and spirituality bear these names, thereby showing the ultimate achievement of learning. From greatness to sagehood and spirituality, all are the fullest realization of a single principle. Yet without learning, how could one gradually attain them? Mencius seems to mean this: principle within us runs through the highest and lowest alike as a unity. It is through learning alone that one gradually advances toward its utmost realization; this, then, is where the gentleman should exert himself.
Thus one begins with goodness and sincerity, developing these until one has attained greatness. The flourishing of one’s virtue and accomplishments would seem unsurpassable. Yet if one remains bound to discernible traces, this is still something anyone can attain. Only by attaining greatness and continuing one’s efforts without cease can inward cultivation benefit from profound attainment, until there is simply no need for deliberate effort to hold fast to and preserve the mind; and outward practice acquire the ease of being securely established, until it is wholly free of dependence on deliberate cultivation. What is called greatness then has virtually no visible traces. This is to accord effortlessly with the Way, without deliberation or exertion, acting through Heaven rather than through human contrivance. Who but the utmost sage under Heaven could participate in this?
From greatness and transformation one proceeds to the ultimate, accumulating attainment until sagehood is reached. It would seem that the workings of thought had nowhere further to advance. Yet if one remained confined to a fixed mode, then …

translation_en:
…it too would be something anyone could accomplish. Only when the sage does not display his functioning is his consummate virtue profound and subtle: probe the source of what he preserves and holds fast within, and its beginning cannot be found; exhaustively investigate the functioning through which his naturally perfected nature is put into practice, and its limits cannot be reached. What is called sagehood is scarcely fathomable through knowledge. Such a person has neither fixed direction nor fixed form; his virtue accords with yin and yang. He works wondrously among things without being confined by them. Who but one of the utmost spiritual attainment in the world could participate in this? Thus, although the names ‘spiritual’ and ‘sage’ seem different, the principle leading from sagehood to spiritual attainment is one and the same. Both assuredly take goodness and sincerity as their foundation. How, then, should learners exert themselves? In essence, learning serves to fulfill one’s nature; the sage shares the same fundamental nature as other people, and sagehood and spiritual attainment are not virtues cut off from theirs. Yet ordinary people follow this without knowing it, while exemplary men hold fast to it without achieving transformation. Thus, in the end, none attain it. Master Xun Qing said: ‘Learning begins with becoming a scholar and ends with becoming a sage.’ Those who aspire to this may encourage themselves with these words.

‘In Inner Sincerity, it is through beneficial correctness that one responds to Heaven.’

Associate Examiner Tang, Senior Compiler, comments: ‘Its wording is concise, yet its treatment of principle is comprehensive. Its explanation of responding to Heaven is especially clear and precise. It merits inclusion.’

translation_en:
…is still more penetrating at this point; this is a work pure in its understanding of the Changes.

Associate Examiner Dong, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: “Purity, refinement, and subtlety constitute the teaching of the Changes. This composition captures them and should serve as a model for the many candidates.”

Examiner Yin, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “Its exposition of principle is clear and lucid.”

Examiner Li, Grand Secretary, comments: “Pure and correct, fluent and perspicuous.”

The Commentary on the Judgments invokes the correctness of Inner Sincerity (Zhongfu) and speaks of its accord with Heaven. The Way of Heaven is utterly trustworthy and invariably correct. The correctness of Inner Sincerity takes this as its basis; surely this enables it to accord with Heaven! What is prized in the Way is trustworthiness; what people prize in trustworthiness is correctness. Trustworthiness without correctness is not a path the gentleman follows. When Inner Sincerity says, “It is beneficial to be correct,” this means that whatever is rooted in freedom from falsity is measured against principle before it moves, and whatever issues forth without deception is tested against righteousness before it acts. Trustworthiness has no fixed substance: it takes correctness as its substance, so that what is preserved within does not become mired in the selfishness of arbitrary suppositions and insistence on foregone conclusions. Trustworthiness has no constant function: it takes correctness as its function, so that what manifests outwardly is not encumbered by the partiality of obstinacy and self-centeredness. Being thus, how could it fail to accord with Heaven?

Profound and unceasing, proceeding with constancy—such is Heaven’s trustworthiness. Pure and refined, moving without stagnation—such is the correctness of its trustworthiness. When inner sincerity makes correctness beneficial, what follows one’s nature is already grounded in real principle, without admixture; what is accomplished in conduct naturally accords with Heaven’s mind and truly conforms to it. Preserved within, it is both trustworthy and correct: before being stirred, it is a single, firmly settled foundation of stillness and concentration, which may be established without contravening Heaven. Expressed outwardly, it is both trustworthy and correct: once it has been stirred…

…an all-embracing functioning, direct in its activity, can flow together with Heaven. Would this not be called responding to Heaven? Ah! The principle of trustworthiness and correctness extends to Heaven; human beings assuredly cannot depart from it. The hexagram statement says, “It is beneficial to be steadfast and correct.” There is good reason for this! Indeed, Heaven’s genuine principle is precisely the genuine heart of human beings. Only when people themselves lose their trustworthiness and correctness do they cease to resemble Heaven. Is not the steadfast correctness of Inner Truth (Zhongfu) the learning of skillfully returning to oneself? Thus it is said, “Knowing how to serve one’s heart is knowing how to serve Heaven.”

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
大傳極賛造化德業而必推原其盛大焉甚矣
造化德業之極其盛大也然不自其富有日新
者觀之抑何以知其然哉今夫造化之理无形
而氣機之運有常故即顯藏之妙可以徵德業
之至矣彼顯仁以鼓氣機之出也萬物莫不隨
之以出是其蓄諸內者充足而无不有德莫有
盛之矣然時至而氣與之通造化何心焉无心
之德斯為德之至乎藏用以鼓氣機之入也萬
物莫不隨之以入是其發于外者周徧而无不
被業莫有大之矣然時往而氣與之復造化何
心焉無心之業斯為業之至乎夫業在外者也
藏用何言乎大業盖措諸外必本諸內其含之
也弘故其施之也不匱則藏用非大業也而藏
用之富有者固大業所由基矣德在內者也顯
仁何言乎盛德盖有諸內必形諸外其積之也
深故其出之也不窮則顯仁非盛德也而顯仁
之日新者固盛德所為徵矣夫德業相因而陰
陽合一此道之妙而易之所以為至歟抑天地

punctuated: 大傳極賛造化德業，而必推原其盛大焉。甚矣，造化德業之極其盛大也！然不自其富有日新者觀之，抑何以知其然哉？今夫造化之理无形，而氣機之運有常，故即顯藏之妙，可以徵德業之至矣。彼顯仁以鼓氣機之出也，萬物莫不隨之以出，是其蓄諸內者充足而无不有，德莫有盛之矣。然時至而氣與之通，造化何心焉？无心之德，斯為德之至乎！藏用以鼓氣機之入也，萬物莫不隨之以入，是其發于外者周徧而无不被，業莫有大之矣。然時往而氣與之復，造化何心焉？無心之業，斯為業之至乎！夫業在外者也，藏用何言乎大業？盖措諸外必本諸內，其含之也弘，故其施之也不匱。則藏用非大業也，而藏用之富有者，固大業所由基矣。德在內者也，顯仁何言乎盛德？盖有諸內必形諸外，其積之也深，故其出之也不窮。則顯仁非盛德也，而顯仁之日新者，固盛德所為徵矣。夫德業相因，而陰陽合一，此道之妙，而易之所以為至歟？抑天地
translation_en:
The Great Commentary praises to the utmost the virtue and achievement of the creative transformations of nature, invariably tracing them to their fullness and greatness. How supremely full and great are nature’s virtue and achievement! Yet unless we consider its abundant possession and daily renewal, how can we know that this is so? The principle of nature’s creative transformations is formless, while the workings of its vital force follow a constant course. Thus, through the subtlety of manifestation and concealment, we can discern the perfection of its virtue and achievement.

In manifesting benevolence, it impels the outward movement of vital force, and all things follow it in emerging. What it stores within is thus ample and lacks nothing: no virtue surpasses this in fullness. Yet when the time arrives, vital force flows forth accordingly. What deliberate intention does nature have? Surely virtue without deliberate intention is virtue at its utmost! In concealing its operation, it impels the inward movement of vital force, and all things follow it in withdrawing. What it sends forth outward thus reaches everywhere and leaves nothing untouched: no achievement surpasses this in greatness. Yet when the time passes, vital force returns accordingly. What deliberate intention does nature have? Surely achievement without deliberate intention is achievement at its utmost!

Achievement belongs to the outward realm. Why, then, speak of concealing operation in connection with great achievement? What is put into effect outwardly must be rooted within. Because what it contains is vast, what it bestows is inexhaustible. Concealing operation is therefore not itself great achievement, but the abundant possession involved in concealing operation is indeed the foundation of great achievement. Virtue belongs to the inward realm. Why, then, speak of manifesting benevolence in connection with full virtue? What exists within must take form outwardly. Because what it accumulates is deep, what issues from it is unending. Manifesting benevolence is therefore not itself full virtue, but the daily renewal involved in manifesting benevolence is indeed the evidence of full virtue.

Virtue and achievement depend upon one another, and yin and yang unite as one. Is this not the subtlety of the Way and the reason the Changes is supremely perfect? Moreover, Heaven and Earth…

Thus daily renewal is precisely the sage’s virtue, and abundant possession is precisely the sage’s achievement. title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
德之盛也盖以德化民治之極也有虞君臣專
尚德教兹其治之弗可及歟今夫察政治之原
而後可以語尚德之化通幽明之故而後可以
語感應之幾故益之贊禹以為不可度者神也
而所可格者誠也苟有明信則念慮所及自潛
孚於對越之時雖無常享而精神所感自昭著
於陟降之頃是至誠之道神且不違而況於苗
民乎益盖深知夫帝德廣運信有以致大順之
化而有苗未格不足以為極治之累矣真盛德
===
之言也禹則拜而俞之敬有所加禮雖恭而不
過理有所契應之速而無疑於是班師振旅若
不知逆命之非而舍已從人誠有得於昌言之
啓矣斯時也帝則夫何為哉但見其不顯篤恭
之妙而文命之敷於四海者溢然好生之德也
樂觀道化之成而干羽之舞於兩階者藹然揖
讓之風也至治運於無為太和昭於有象虞廷
之盛可想見哉七旬有苗格宜矣雖然徂征誓
師非聖人意也至誠之謨益固陳之舜禹先得

translation_en:
…the flourishing of virtue. For transforming the people through virtue is the highest achievement of government. The ruler and ministers of Yu devoted themselves exclusively to moral instruction: was this why their government could not be surpassed? Only after examining the source of political order can one discuss the transforming influence of honoring virtue; only after comprehending the workings of the unseen and visible realms can one discuss the subtle beginnings of stimulus and response. Thus, in assisting Yu, Yi held that the spirits cannot be fathomed, yet sincerity can reach them. If one possesses luminous good faith, whatever one’s thoughts encompass will silently establish communion as one stands before the spirits. Though they do not invariably accept offerings, the influence of one’s vital spirit will become manifest as they ascend and descend. Such is the Way of utmost sincerity: even the spirits do not oppose it, much less the Miao people! Yi surely understood deeply that the emperor’s virtue extended far and operated widely, and could indeed bring about a transformation toward complete accord. That the Youmiao had not yet submitted was insufficient to mar this consummate government. These truly were words of abundant virtue!

Yu bowed and assented. His reverence increased: though his observance of ritual was deferential, it was not excessive. Recognizing the accord with principle, he responded swiftly and without hesitation. He therefore withdrew and marshaled his troops, as though unaware of the wrong of defying his commands. In setting aside his own judgment [?] and following another’s, he had truly benefited from the enlightenment offered by excellent counsel. At this time, what did the emperor himself do? One sees only the subtle efficacy of his unobtrusive, profound reverence: his civilizing instruction, spread throughout the Four Seas, overflowed with the virtue of cherishing life. He delighted in witnessing the fulfillment of moral transformation: the dance with shields and feathers between the two stairways exuded the spirit of deference and yielding. Consummate government operated through nonaction; supreme harmony shone forth in visible forms. How vividly one can imagine the flourishing court of Yu! It was fitting that after seventy days the Youmiao submitted. Nevertheless, marching on campaign and addressing the troops with an oath were not what the sage intended. Yi certainly set forth the counsel of utmost sincerity, but Shun and Yu had already grasped…

已至篤棐永念予之賴於公者無窮公稱丕顯
德豈特以予揚文武烈哉是故繼文武而仰膺
天命之隆予之責重矣公則以予奉答之不永
為戒而敢不敬者聿端出治之本恒吉其貞而
罔不若者重宣昭受之光基命以成始也迓天
休於滋至定命以成終也衍帝曆於無疆自今
日至於萬年天之眷予者庶有以答之而無愧

悠久而離逖者同歸於必世之仁棐之民彝而
相協厥居也迪之吉康而綏爰有眾也由王畿
達之四方民之戴予者庶有以奠之而不怍矣
使非公輔之則難保之民何以安哉然則公之
去留固天命民心之所係而可求去乎抑論民

…has already reached its utmost extent. Through your earnest assistance and enduring concern, my reliance upon you, Duke, is without limit. When you speak of greatly manifesting virtue, can you mean merely that I should proclaim the achievements of Kings Wen and Wu? Thus, in succeeding Wen and Wu and reverently receiving Heaven’s exalted mandate, my responsibility is weighty indeed. You caution me against failing to respond to Heaven enduringly. How could I dare to be irreverent [?]? Thereby I rectify the foundation from which government proceeds. By remaining steadfast in what is auspicious and correct, with nothing contrary to it, I renew and make manifest the glory of what I have illustriously received. Establishing the mandate to accomplish the beginning, I welcome Heaven’s blessings in increasing abundance; securing the mandate to accomplish the end, I extend the dynasty’s allotted span without limit. From this day through ten thousand years, I may thus have the means to requite Heaven’s favor toward me without shame. Without your assistance, how could I serve Heaven, which is so difficult to trust?

In succeeding Wen and Wu and receiving responsibility for the multitude of living people below, my responsibility is weighty indeed. Through you, my government of enduring harmony grows in generosity and abundance [?], and the unruly are quietly won over by its universally harmonizing influence. As the Way is realized and endures, even those estranged and far removed come together under the benevolence that requires a generation to achieve. You support the people’s constant moral principles and help them live together harmoniously; you guide them toward good fortune and well-being and bring peace to these multitudes. From the royal domain to the four quarters, I may thus have the means to settle the people who uphold me, without shame. Without your assistance, how could I bring peace to the people, whose allegiance is so difficult to retain? Your departure or continued presence is therefore bound up with Heaven’s mandate and the people’s hearts. How, then, can you seek to leave?

When the people’s hearts were pleased, Heaven’s approval was obtained. The means to accomplish this, however, lay in ruler and minister being of one mind. Consider how King Cheng revered virtue and dealt sincerely with the people, while the Duke of Zhou amply protected the people entrusted to him. text:
之不可忘備也周王修講武之事則所以保治
者有道矣宜諸侯之美之與且夫王者之制治
也有文德以昭其盛則必有武備以防其衰我
君子之講武于洛也豈特福禄之同已哉惟兹
家邦造自文武盖萬年之丕基也永言保之則
繼體者之責耳惟我君子德懋剛中光撫盈成
之業幾先明炳深惟理亂之原仁義禮樂之化
固足以結民心矣而六師之作所為遏不靖之
萌者欲制治於無疆焉紀綱法度之施固足以
===
定民志矣而戎兵之詰所為振不競之漸者將
圖大於有永焉百辟承式今之家邦幸安也儆
戒無虞使延之萬年而益安則承式者不怠而
國體有常尊之勢矣四夷来王今之家邦幸寧
也思患預防使延之萬年而愈寧則来王者罔
後而宗社有靈長之慶矣吁修武備於平時而
諸侯與天子同志此周道所以盛乎抑武王遷
鎬首建辟雝而天下服此獨拳拳于武事何耶
盖治平既久則武備易弛以時講修固安不忘

圖大於有永焉百辟承式令之家邦幸安也儆
戒無虞使延之萬年而益安則承式者不怠而
國體有常尊之勢矣四夷來王令之家邦幸寧
也思患預防使延之萬年而愈寧則來王者罔
後而宗社有靈長之慶矣吁修武備於平時而
諸侯與天子同志此周道所以盛乎抑武王遷
鎬首建辟雍而天下服此獨拳拳于武事何耶
蓋治平既久則武備易弛以時講修固安不忘
punctuated: 之不可忘備也！周王修講武之事，則所以保治者有道矣，宜諸侯之美之與！且夫王者之制治也，有文德以昭其盛，則必有武備以防其衰。我君子之講武于洛也，豈特福禄之同已哉？惟兹家邦，造自文武，盖萬年之丕基也。永言保之，則繼體者之責耳。惟我君子，德懋剛中，光撫盈成之業；幾先明炳，深惟理亂之原。仁義禮樂之化，固足以結民心矣，而六師之作，所為遏不靖之萌者，欲制治於無疆焉。紀綱法度之施，固足以定民志矣，而戎兵之詰，所為振不競之漸者，將圖大於有永焉。百辟承式，今之家邦幸安也；儆戒無虞，使延之萬年而益安，則承式者不怠，而國體有常尊之勢矣。四夷来王，今之家邦幸寧也；思患預防，使延之萬年而愈寧，則来王者罔後，而宗社有靈長之慶矣。吁！修武備於平時，而諸侯與天子同志，此周道所以盛乎！抑武王遷鎬，首建辟雝而天下服，此獨拳拳于武事何耶？盖治平既久，則武備易弛，以時講修，固安不忘
translation_en:
…that preparedness must never be forgotten amid peace and good order! By attending to military exercises, the king of Zhou had a proper means of preserving good government. How fitting that the feudal lords should praise him! When a king establishes order, if he possesses civil virtue to display its flourishing, he must also maintain military preparedness to guard against its decline. When our lord held military exercises at Luo, was it merely to share blessings and good fortune? This royal house and realm, founded by Kings Wen and Wu, constituted a mighty foundation for ten thousand years. To preserve it forever was the responsibility of their successors. Our lord’s virtue flourished in firmness and balance, and he gloriously sustained an inheritance already brought to fullness and accomplishment. His insight shone clearly before events took shape, and he pondered deeply the sources of order and disorder. The transforming influence of benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music was indeed sufficient to bind the people’s hearts to him. Yet he mobilized the Six Armies to suppress the first stirrings of unrest, seeking thereby to establish order without end. The implementation of governing principles, laws, and institutions was indeed sufficient to settle the people’s minds. Yet he put weapons and troops in readiness to arrest an incipient decline in strength, intending thereby to secure greatness for all time.

The many lords followed his example: the royal house and realm were now fortunately secure. By remaining vigilant when there was no cause for alarm, and extending that security through ten thousand years so that it grew still greater, those who followed his example would remain diligent, and the dignity of the state would command enduring respect. The peoples of the four quarters came to acknowledge his kingship: the royal house and realm were now fortunately at peace. By contemplating troubles and guarding against them in advance, and extending that peace through ten thousand years so that it grew still deeper, none would lag behind in coming to acknowledge his kingship, and the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain would enjoy the blessing of enduring vitality. Ah! Military preparedness was maintained in peacetime, and the feudal lords shared the Son of Heaven’s purpose. Was this not why the Way of Zhou flourished?

Yet when King Wu moved to Hao, he first established the Biyong, the royal ritual college, and all under Heaven submitted. Why, here, was such earnest attention devoted solely to military affairs? Because, after peace and order have long prevailed, military preparedness readily grows lax. To conduct exercises and attend to it at proper intervals is indeed, while secure, not to forget…

translation_en:
…the way of remembering danger amid security. When we examine “ luxuriant Are the Flowers” (Shang shang zhe hua), which makes manifest virtue the source of blessings, we see that the Zhou ruler and his ministers also had their own way of jointly planning for the realm through their exchanges of counsel and response. How could they have relied exclusively on military preparedness?
“The phoenixes call upon that high ridge; the parasol trees grow upon that sunward slope. Luxuriant and flourishing are the trees; harmonious and melodious are the calls.”
Feng Qian
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Chief Supervising Secretary: “The language is gentle and the intent earnest, attaining the proper manner for addressing a ruler. Accept it.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Chief Supervising Secretary: “The language and reasoning are clear and lucid; the admonition is gently conveyed.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Hanlin Compiler: “The poem employs analogy because it does not wish to state its meaning explicitly. Once that meaning is spelled out, it becomes shallow. This composition is suggestive and rich in implication, capturing the original intent of Duke Kang of Shao in admonishing King Cheng to employ worthy men. Accept it.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Hanlin Senior Compiler: “The topic is straightforward, and most writers repeat conventional phrases. This piece alone displays clarity, refinement, and classical elegance. Reading it gives the effect of one voice singing and three responding in admiration.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Ji, Hanlin Senior Compiler: “The wording and meaning are gentle yet earnest, capturing the Duke of Shao’s loyal and loving concern.”
Comment by Examiner Yin, Hanlin Expositor-in-Waiting: “Uniquely accomplished in subtlety and gentleness.”
Comment by Examiner Li, Grand Secretary: “Rich in lasting significance and savor.”

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
□臣陳戒必即物以况君臣之感合焉甚矣君
臣感合之難也大臣即物以陳戒啓君之道何
至哉召康公從成王卷阿之遊而矢音至此若
曰物類之相附集者機也君臣之相感合者道
也王其即物而動思乎彼鳳凰為鳥之靈而出
之必以時也今則于高岡鳴焉昭曠以賁其
文明盖盛世之覩為禎祥者矣梧桐為木之美
而植之貴得所也今則于朝陽生焉蔭高朗以
蕃其枝本盖靈鳥之托為依棲者矣時至而物
===
滋則見夫在朝陽者蓁蓁而萋萋也葉之沃若
既茂乎日夜之息焉氣和而聲應則見夫在高
岡者雝雝而喈喈也音之載好自得乎翔止之
儀焉生之盛而鳴之和感之神而應之速若有
以使之然者吾王遊歌適情而物類之在目焉
盍亦觸思而求其故哉盖君之於臣恩禮隆洽
欲興其嚮用之心而臣之於君謀猷協輔期答
夫遭逢之數與此正相類耳噫召公斯詩亦有
味乎其言之與嘗觀鹿鳴諸詩見成王於臣誠

滋則見夫在朝陽者菶菶而萋萋也葉之沃若
旣茂乎日夜之息焉氣和而聲應則見夫在高

儀焉生之盛而鳴之和感之神而應之速若有

盍亦觸思而求其故哉蓋君之於臣恩禮隆洽
欲興其嚮用之心而臣之於君謀猷協輔期晉
夫遭逢之數與此正相類耳噫召公斯詩亦有
味乎其言之與嘗觀賡鳴諸詩見成王於臣誠
punctuated:
□臣陳戒，必即物以况君臣之感合焉。甚矣，君臣感合之難也！大臣即物以陳戒，啓君之道何至哉！召康公從成王卷阿之遊而矢音至此，若曰：「物類之相附集者，機也；君臣之相感合者，道也。王其即物而動思乎！彼鳳凰為鳥之靈，而出之必以時也。今則于高岡鳴焉，昭曠以賁其文明，盖盛世之覩為禎祥者矣。梧桐為木之美，而植之貴得所也。今則于朝陽生焉，蔭高朗以蕃其枝本，盖靈鳥之托為依棲者矣。時至而物滋，則見夫在朝陽者蓁蓁而萋萋也。葉之沃若，既茂乎日夜之息焉。氣和而聲應，則見夫在高岡者雝雝而喈喈也。音之載好，自得乎翔止之儀焉。生之盛而鳴之和，感之神而應之速，若有以使之然者。吾王遊歌適情，而物類之在目焉，盍亦觸思而求其故哉？盖君之於臣，恩禮隆洽，欲興其嚮用之心；而臣之於君，謀猷協輔，期答夫遭逢之數，與此正相類耳。」
噫！召公斯詩，亦有味乎其言之與！嘗觀《鹿鳴》諸詩，見成王於臣誠
translation_en:
…[?] When a minister presents admonitions, he invariably draws upon things to illustrate the mutual responsiveness and concord of ruler and ministers. How difficult it is for ruler and ministers to achieve such concord! How consummate is the great minister’s way of enlightening his ruler by drawing upon things to present admonitions! Duke Kang of Shao accompanied King Cheng on his excursion to the winding hill and gave voice to his verse at this point, as if to say: “What brings creatures together in mutual attachment is their spontaneous impulse; what brings ruler and ministers into responsive concord is the Way. May the king reflect upon the things before him! The phoenix is the numinous one among birds, and it appears only at the proper time. Now it cries upon the high ridge, where the open brightness enhances its brilliant markings: surely its appearance in a flourishing age is an auspicious sign. The wutong is a fine tree, and in planting it, finding the right place is essential. Now it grows on the sunward slope, spreading shade over that high, bright place and flourishing in branch and trunk: surely it offers the numinous bird a place to settle and roost. When the season arrives and things flourish, we see those trees on the sunward slope growing dense and luxuriant. Their glossy leaves flourish through growth by day and night. When the vital forces are harmonious and voices respond, we hear those birds upon the high ridge calling in harmonious accord. Their beautiful notes come naturally amid their graceful flight and rest. Such luxuriant growth and harmonious cries, such wondrous responsiveness and swift answering, seem to have something that makes them so. As our king takes pleasure in excursions and song, with these creatures before his eyes, why should he not let them stir his reflections and seek the reason for this? The ruler extends abundant favor and courtesy to his ministers, wishing to inspire their readiness to serve; the ministers assist their ruler with concerted counsel, hoping to repay the good fortune of having found him. This is precisely analogous to what we see here.”
Ah! How much there is to savor in the words of this poem by the Duke of Shao! Having read ‘The Deer Call’ and the associated poems, I have seen how King Cheng, toward his ministers, was sincere…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
意懇至而禮遇周渥蓁萋之喻盖已說而繹之
矣當時受賜諸臣歌天保以獻其忠則亦庶幾
雝喈之音焉故曰太和盛治在成周宇宙間信
已然則召康公啓助之力豈少哉
春秋
齊人伐山戎莊公三十年六月齊侯來
獻戎捷莊公三十有一年
耿定向

===

punctuated:
意懇至，而禮遇周渥，蓁萋之喻，盖已說而繹之矣。當時受賜諸臣，歌天保以獻其忠，則亦庶幾雝喈之音焉。故曰：「太和盛治在成周宇宙間。」信已！然則召康公啓助之力豈少哉？

春秋
「齊人伐山戎。」莊公三十年。「六月，齊侯來獻戎捷。」莊公三十有一年。
耿定向

同考試官主事況批：「聖人抑戎捷，正不欲其遠伐也。此作獨能發明，深得傳意，可以式矣。」
同考試官侍讀瞿批：「伐戎獻捷，本一事，春秋貶齊桓之意亦互見，此作得之。」
考試官侍講學士尹批：「得聖人抑桓意。」
考試官大學士李批：「辭嚴義正。」

春秋于伯主，始因其伐遠而譏之，復因其矜功而抑之。夫勤兵于遠，勝之非所以為功也。齊桓兩失之，此春秋重貶之以示戒歟？且伐山戎者，齊侯也。君親在行，非將卑而師少也。伐而稱人，
translation_en:
…his intentions were deeply earnest, and his courteous treatment comprehensive and generous: the metaphor of luxuriant growth has already explained and elaborated this. The ministers who received his gifts then sang Heaven Protects You (Tian bao) to offer their loyalty; this, too, approached the harmonious sounds of the phoenixes. Thus it is said, “Perfect harmony and flourishing government prevailed throughout the world of Chengzhou.” True indeed! Could Duke Kang of Shao’s contribution in guiding and assisting the king, then, have been slight?

Spring and Autumn Annals
“The men of Qi attacked the Mountain Rong.” Thirtieth year of Duke Zhuang.
“In the sixth month, the Marquis of Qi came to present the spoils of victory over the Rong.” Thirty-first year of Duke Zhuang.
Geng Dingxiang

Associate Examiner Kuang, Secretary, comments: “In disparaging the presentation of spoils from the Rong, the Sage precisely intended to oppose campaigning so far afield. This composition alone brings this out clearly and grasps the commentary’s meaning profoundly. It can serve as a model.”
Associate Examiner Qu, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Attacking the Rong and presenting the spoils are essentially one affair. The Spring and Autumn Annals’ intention to censure Duke Huan of Qi also emerges through the two entries read together. This composition grasps that.”
Examiner Yin, Expositor-in-Waiting Academician, comments: “It grasps the Sage’s intention to disparage Duke Huan.”
Examiner Li, Grand Secretary, comments: “The language is stern and the principles upright.”

In its treatment of the hegemon, the Spring and Autumn Annals first criticizes him for campaigning far afield, then disparages him again for boasting of his achievement. To wear out troops in distant lands, even in victory, is no basis for claiming merit. Duke Huan of Qi erred on both counts. Is this why the Spring and Autumn Annals censures him twice, to furnish a warning? Moreover, the one who attacked the Mountain Rong was the Marquis of Qi. The ruler personally accompanied the expedition; this was no case of a low-ranking commander and a small army. Yet in recording the attack, it calls them “men”…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
君子以為譏之者何也盖內夏外夷者先王之
制以荒漠之地而動節制之師非所以安內也
山戎雖病燕然非門庭之宼齊侯欲耀武于戎
乃勞吾民而肆伐焉則其舉事也為喜功其深
入也為窮兵矣春秋懼後人之藉口于是役也
故特貶而稱人以其事不足稱而故微之也不
然則薄伐玁狁周宣之所以為烈也是伐亦近
之矣而何譏焉及其師旋獻戎捷者亦齊侯也
齊固方伯非能屈己以下魯也捷而稱獻君子
===
以為抑之者何也盖耀德不觀兵者先王之制
以無名之師而有倖成之功非所以誇人也山
戎雖就俘然非王愾之敵齊侯欲示威于魯乃
陳軍獲而奏凱焉則勞不足以定國而居之也
驕禮不足以制心而施之也悖矣春秋懼後人
之藉口于是捷也故特貶而稱獻以其功不足
多而故卑之也不然則以奏膚功吉甫之所以
為賢也是捷亦類之矣而又何抑焉此義明則
人君圖治近政在所先而遠畧無足貴矣文德

多而故畀之也不然則以奏膚功吉甫之所以
爲賢也是捷亦類之矣而又何抑焉此義明則
人君圖治近政在所先而遠畧無足貴矣文德
punctuated: 君子以為譏之者何也？盖內夏外夷者，先王之制。以荒漠之地而動節制之師，非所以安內也。山戎雖病燕，然非門庭之宼。齊侯欲耀武于戎，乃勞吾民而肆伐焉，則其舉事也為喜功，其深入也為窮兵矣。春秋懼後人之藉口于是役也，故特貶而稱人，以其事不足稱而故微之也。不然，則薄伐玁狁，周宣之所以為烈也，是伐亦近之矣，而何譏焉？及其師旋，獻戎捷者亦齊侯也。齊固方伯，非能屈己以下魯也。捷而稱獻，君子以為抑之者何也？盖耀德不觀兵者，先王之制。以無名之師而有倖成之功，非所以誇人也。山戎雖就俘，然非王愾之敵。齊侯欲示威于魯，乃陳軍獲而奏凱焉，則勞不足以定國而居之也驕，禮不足以制心而施之也悖矣。春秋懼後人之藉口于是捷也，故特貶而稱獻，以其功不足多而故卑之也。不然，則以奏膚功，吉甫之所以為賢也，是捷亦類之矣，而又何抑焉？此義明，則人君圖治，近政在所先，而遠畧無足貴矣。文德
translation_en:
…Why do discerning gentlemen regard this as criticism of him? Treating the Xia as the inner realm and the non-Chinese peoples as outside it was the established rule of the former kings. Mobilizing a disciplined army for the sake of a desolate territory is no way to secure the inner realm. Although the Shanrong afflicted Yan, they were not raiders at Qi’s own gates. The Marquis of Qi wished to flaunt his military might among the Rong, so he wore out our people in an unrestrained campaign against them. Thus, undertaking this action amounted to a craving for achievement, and penetrating deep into their territory amounted to exhausting his military resources. The Spring and Autumn Annals feared that later generations would invoke this campaign as a pretext. It therefore expressly degraded him by calling him merely a “man”: because his undertaking did not deserve praise, it deliberately diminished him. Otherwise, campaigning against the Xianyun was what made King Xuan of Zhou illustrious; this campaign was similar, so why criticize it?

When the army returned, it was likewise the Marquis of Qi who presented the spoils of victory over the Rong. Qi was, after all, the leader of the regional lords, and he was not one to humble himself before Lu. Why do discerning gentlemen regard the description of his victory as a “presentation” as a way of lowering him? Displaying virtue rather than military force was the established rule of the former kings. A success achieved by good fortune with an army lacking a legitimate cause is no ground for boasting before others. Although the Shanrong had been taken captive, they were not enemies who had incurred the king’s wrath. The Marquis of Qi wished to display his power before Lu, so he exhibited his army’s captures and performed the music of victory. His exertions were insufficient to bring stability to the state, yet he arrogantly claimed credit for them; his ritual observance was insufficient to restrain his heart, and his performance of it was perverse. The Spring and Autumn Annals feared that later generations would invoke this victory as a pretext. It therefore expressly degraded him by calling it a “presentation”: because his achievement did not deserve great esteem, it deliberately lowered him. Otherwise, “thereby accomplishing a great achievement” was what made Jifu worthy; this victory was similar, so why again lower him?

Once this principle is understood, a ruler seeking good government will give priority to governing what is near, while distant campaigns will have nothing worthy of esteem. Civil virtue…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
在所修而武功無足貪矣彼有敝中國而事夷
狄者其不明春秋之義乎雖然楚亦山戎等耳
召陵何以獨美之也漢陽諸姬楚實盡之且僭
王矣微齊桓中國幾何不胥而為夷也若山戎
豈其微而無係于中國之盛衰乎春秋之美召
陵盖不得已也然齊桓不務德而勤遠畧為宰
孔所窺此齊桓之事孔門所以不道乎
季孫斯仲孫何忌帥師墮費定公十有二年
常三省
===

考試官大學士李批得聖人之意
觀大夫之革僭邑而聖人以禮為國之兆見矣
夫禮所以經國家也聖人一言而費以墮禮之
不可巳也如此夫且季孫曷為而墮費也有感

translation_en:
…is what must be cultivated, while military achievements are not worth coveting. Those who exhaust the Central States in campaigns against the Yi and Di—do they not fail to understand the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals? Yet Chu was merely another power like the Shanrong; why, then, does the Annals praise the expedition to Shaoling alone? Chu had indeed extinguished all the Ji-surnamed states north of the Han River and had even usurped the royal title. Without Duke Huan of Qi, how close would the Central States have come to becoming barbarians together? As for the Shanrong, could it be that they were insignificant and had no bearing on the rise or decline of the Central States? [?] The Annals’ praise of Shaoling was surely unavoidable. Yet Duke Huan of Qi neglected virtue and devoted himself to distant campaigns, a failing that Zai Kong discerned. Is this why the school of Confucius did not speak of Duke Huan’s deeds?
“Jisun Si and Zhongsun Heji led troops to demolish the fortifications of Fei.” The twelfth year of Duke Ding.
Chang Sansheng
Comment by Associate Examiner Kuang, a Secretary: “The writing is disciplined and rigorous. Introducing ritual propriety at the outset shows insight in the argument.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Qu, a Reader-in-waiting: “The discussion of the Sage’s governing the state through ritual propriety is clear and incisive, and deserves praise.”
Comment by Examiner Yin, a Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting: “The exposition is orderly and polished.”
Comment by Examiner Li, a Grand Secretary: “It grasps the Sage’s intent.”
In observing the great officers’ dismantling of an unlawfully fortified town, we see signs of the Sage’s governing the state through ritual propriety. Ritual propriety is the means by which the state is ordered. With a single utterance from the Sage, Fei’s fortifications were demolished: such is the indispensability of ritual propriety! Why, then, did Jisun demolish Fei’s fortifications? He was moved…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
于孔子之言也在禮私家不藏甲邑城無百雉
所以辨上下而定民志也費之不度越禮甚矣
始也季氏挾之以弱魯而為公室之憂既也陪
臣挾之以叛季而為私室之患雖季氏亦悔之
矣孔子因季孫之訪而正之以禮盖因其悔悟
之機而寓吾撥亂之權也于是乎季孫仲孫帥
師而墮費焉仲由謀之而負固者莫能抗申句
須樂頎伐之而怙終者莫能格百年之弊革于
一旦公室之復張諸侯得以保其國而不憂于
===
末大者在此舉也數世之患定于俄頃私室之
亦安大夫得以保其家而不患于效尤者亦在
此舉也夫子謹禮之言一出而費邑墮由是而
知禮之可以已亂也夫子之道之可行此為之
兆矣使得究其志則諸侯不敢越禮以侵小大
夫不敢越禮以封殖安生于上下之分定而魯
其東周矣又豈止于一費之墮乎雖然魯郊非
禮則三家之僭魯亦有以取之非獨三家之尤
也夫子用禮之志且將以張公室者而尊周□
