punctuated: 于孔子之言也。在禮，私家不藏甲，邑城無百雉，所以辨上下而定民志也。費之不度，越禮甚矣。始也，季氏挾之以弱魯，而為公室之憂；既也，陪臣挾之以叛季，而為私室之患，雖季氏亦悔之矣。孔子因季孫之訪，而正之以禮，盖因其悔悟之機，而寓吾撥亂之權也。于是乎季孫、仲孫帥師而墮費焉。仲由謀之，而負固者莫能抗；申句須、樂頎伐之，而怙終者莫能格。百年之弊革于一旦，公室之復張，諸侯得以保其國而不憂于末大者，在此舉也。數世之患定于俄頃，私室之亦安，大夫得以保其家而不患于效尤者，亦在此舉也。夫子謹禮之言一出而費邑墮，由是而知禮之可以已亂也。夫子之道之可行，此為之兆矣。使得究其志，則諸侯不敢越禮以侵小，大夫不敢越禮以封殖，安生于上下之分定，而魯其東周矣，又豈止于一費之墮乎？雖然，魯郊非禮，則三家之僭，魯亦有以取之，非獨三家之尤也。夫子用禮之志，且將以張公室者而尊周□
translation_en:
…by the words of Confucius. According to ritual, private ministerial houses were not to store armor, and the walls of their towns were not to reach a hundred zhi in length. These provisions distinguished superior from subordinate and settled the people’s minds. Fei’s exceeding the prescribed dimensions was a grave transgression of ritual. At first, the Ji lineage used it to weaken Lu, making it a source of anxiety for the ducal house. Later, their own retainers used it to rebel against the Ji, making it a threat to that ministerial house. Even the Ji lineage came to regret this. When Jisun consulted Confucius, Confucius set him right through ritual: he seized the opportunity afforded by Jisun’s remorse and awakening to exercise his own power to bring order out of disorder.

Thereupon Jisun and Zhongsun led troops to demolish Fei’s walls. Zhong You planned the operation, and those who relied on its strong defenses could not resist. Shen Juxu and Yue Qi attacked, and those who persisted obstinately in wrongdoing could not withstand them. An abuse of a hundred years was eliminated in a single day. In this action lay the restoration of the ducal house’s strength, enabling the feudal lord to preserve his state without fearing that its subordinate branches would grow too powerful. A trouble of several generations was settled in a moment. In this action also lay the security of the ministerial houses, enabling the great officers to preserve their families without fearing that others would follow the rebels’ bad example.

Once the Master spoke of strict observance of ritual, Fei’s walls were demolished. From this we know that ritual can put an end to disorder. This was a sign that the Master’s Way could be put into practice. Had he been able to fulfill his purpose, the feudal lords would not have dared transgress ritual by invading smaller states, nor would the great officers have dared transgress ritual by building up their own power. Peace would have arisen from clearly established distinctions between superior and subordinate, and Lu would have become a Zhou in the east. How could the result have been limited to the demolition of Fei alone?

Nevertheless, Lu’s suburban sacrifice to Heaven was contrary to ritual. Thus, Lu itself had done something to invite the usurpations of the three ministerial lineages; the fault did not lie with those three lineages alone. In his resolve to apply ritual, the Master further intended to use the strengthening of the ducal house to honor Zhou [?]…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
乎三都之墮盖見諸行事之一初也惜乎定公
不能用費邑既墮而復固則魯之不振而周禮
之不復行皆决于此矣讀春秋能無感乎
禮記
大學之法禁於未發之謂豫當其可之謂
時不陵節而施之謂孫相觀而善之謂摩
此四者教之所由興也

Once the city of Fei had been demolished, it was fortified again. Thus Lu’s failure to recover its strength and the failure to restore the rites of Zhou were both determined at this point. Can one read the Spring and Autumn Annals without being moved?

Book of Rites

“The methods of the Great Learning are these: restraining something before it arises is called prevention; acting at the appropriate moment is called timeliness; imparting instruction without overstepping the stages of learning is called orderly progression; and observing one another and thereby improving is called mutual refinement. Yuan Sui

力易也自其當可而告則謂之時盖善啓於將

punctuated: 事而禁，則謂之豫，盖惡止於未形，斯防之者其力易也。自其當可而告，則謂之時，盖善啓於將達，斯導之者其勢順也。人有分限也，各以其業授之，循序而施，不強其未至，遜所由名焉。友以輔仁也，使觀法而效之，勸率有道，相厲以交修，摩所由名焉。夫是四者，教豈有不興乎？盖為法不同，同歸于身心之益，則持循有地，人不謬於所從；教雖多術，皆妙其鼓舞之機，則進為有方，自不苦其難入。豫以禁之，欲不萌也；時以啓之，理自融也。釋回增美，德日起而有功矣。啓迪之餘，殆勃然而不可已乎！施之以孫，志不亂也；勸之以摩，德不孤也。敬業樂羣，善日進而無疆矣。曲成之下，其油然而莫之禦乎！信乎，大學之法之善也！向使法有未備，則教烏能以興耶？雖然，待教而興者，凡民也。君子之學，能自得師，深造以道，而尚友古人，則道自我立，教自我興矣。法豈在外哉？要之，先王立教之意，亦非專恃乎法者，神而明之，存乎其人耳。故君子欲其自得之
translation_en:
…to prohibit something before it happens is called anticipation. For when wrongdoing is stopped before it takes shape, those guarding against it can do so with little effort. To instruct when the learner is ready is called timeliness. For when goodness is awakened just as understanding is about to dawn, those guiding the learner follow its natural momentum. People have their respective capacities and limits: assign each the appropriate studies and teach in sequence, without forcing them beyond what they have attained. This is why it is called orderly progression. Friends assist one another in benevolence: have learners observe exemplary conduct and emulate it, encourage and guide them properly, and spur one another toward mutual cultivation. This is why it is called mutual polishing. With these four principles, how could education fail to flourish? Although the methods differ, all contribute to the benefit of body and mind. Thus learners have firm ground on which to proceed and do not err in what they follow. Although teaching employs many techniques, all work subtly through opportunities to inspire and encourage. Thus learners have a proper way to advance and do not find entry into learning painfully difficult.

Restrain them through anticipation, and wayward desires will not sprout; awaken them through timely instruction, and principle will naturally become clear. Casting off perversity and increasing what is admirable, their virtue grows daily and bears fruit. Once enlightened and guided, will they not advance vigorously, unable to stop? Teach them through orderly progression, and their aspirations will not become confused; encourage them through mutual polishing, and their virtue will not stand alone. Devoted to their studies and delighting in their companions, they advance in goodness daily without limit. Under instruction that brings each to fulfillment according to individual circumstances, will their growth not proceed naturally, with nothing able to check it? Truly, how excellent are the methods of the Great Learning! Had these methods been incomplete, how could education have flourished?

Nevertheless, it is ordinary people who depend on instruction to rise. In his learning, the gentleman can find teachers for himself, pursue profound attainment by following the Way, and reach back to befriend the ancients. Then the Way is established through oneself, and education flourishes through oneself. How could the method lie outside oneself? Ultimately, the former kings’ intention in establishing education was likewise not to rely exclusively on methods. Making them spiritually effective and illuminating them rests with the person. Thus the gentleman wishes the learner to attain understanding for himself…

運乎太和保合而皆全其性歸根復命而各止
其所作成物者坤也未易以居也夫惟禮出于
自然之序而極充周溥遍之功吾知至序之森
嚴合其因物賦物之精天秩之分辨符其不害
不悖之本天下之物無一非坤之成也則亦無

punctuated:
始，而樂已著乎其初，所以鼓萬物之出機，以彰顯仁之化者，乾不得而專其始矣。樂其與天同運乎？太和保合而皆全其性，歸根復命而各止其所，作成物者坤也，未易以居也。夫惟禮出于自然之序，而極充周溥遍之功，吾知至序之森嚴，合其因物賦物之精；天秩之分辨，符其不害不悖之本。天下之物無一非坤之成也，則亦無一非大禮之管攝。蓋坤作成物，而禮已居乎其位，所以鼓萬物之入機，以彰顯仁之化者，坤不得而專其成矣。禮其與地同功乎？是知乾坤，造化之禮樂也；禮樂，聖人之造化也。聖神功化之極，天地且不能違也，而况于物乎？抑禮樂之理固通乎造化，而實具乎吾心。自其未發而大本立焉，自其已發而達道行焉。所以制作，所以參贊，一以貫之者也。若推其極，則中和非二理，乾坤無二用，非達天人之妙，何足以語此？

第貳場

論
translation_en:
…the beginning, yet music is already manifest at its inception. Thus, in setting in motion the workings through which the myriad things emerge, and thereby manifesting the transforming power of benevolence, Qian cannot claim sole responsibility for their beginning. Does music not move in concert with Heaven? Supreme harmony is preserved and united, and all things fulfill their natures; they return to their roots and revert to their allotted destinies, each coming to rest in its proper place. It is Kun that brings things to completion—a position not easily occupied. Yet ritual issues from the order inherent in nature and fully realizes its all-pervading efficacy. I know that the strict array of perfect order accords with the subtlety whereby each thing is endowed according to what it is; the distinctions of Heaven’s ordering accord with the fundamental principle that things neither harm nor conflict with one another. Among all things under Heaven, none is not completed by Kun; likewise, none lies outside the governance of great ritual. For Kun brings things to completion, yet ritual already occupies its place. Thus, in setting in motion the workings through which the myriad things return inward, and thereby manifesting the transforming power of benevolence, Kun cannot claim sole responsibility for their completion. Does ritual not share in Earth’s work?

From this we know that Qian and Kun are the ritual and music of cosmic creation and transformation, while ritual and music are the sage’s means of creation and transformation. At the highest reach of the transformative achievements of sages and spiritual beings, even Heaven and Earth cannot act contrary to them; how much less can other things? Moreover, although the principles of ritual and music pervade cosmic creation and transformation, they are truly present within our own hearts. Before the feelings are aroused, the great foundation is established there; once they are aroused, the universally applicable Way operates there. The means by which institutions are fashioned and the means by which we participate in and assist cosmic transformation are bound together by a single principle. Pushed to their ultimate point, equilibrium and harmony are not two principles, nor do Qian and Kun have two separate operations. Without comprehending the subtle relationship between Heaven and humanity, how could one be qualified to speak of this?

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Supervising Secretary: The sage’s mind is Heaven’s mind, and its operation is Heaven’s Way. Both are spontaneous and cannot cease; neither depends upon forced effort. This composition elucidates the essential nature of benevolence and profoundly grasps the subtleties of the sage and Heaven’s Way. Its arguments are precise, and its language is classically elegant. Truly an exceptional talent under Heaven! He fully deserves recommendation in first place.

Comment by Associate Examiner Pei, Examining Editor: The sage’s government is rooted in his mind. Those who discuss this often lapse into generalities that miss the point. This composition takes Heaven’s generation of living things as its basis for elucidating the essential nature of benevolence, and its arguments are precise and sound. This is surely someone deeply versed in the Learning of Principle who can also comprehend government. Select him to rank first among the candidates.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xing, Expositor: The sage practices benevolent government with a benevolent mind, fundamentally taking Heaven as his model and establishing the supreme standard. Thus his benevolence can shelter all under Heaven. This composition bases its argument on the essential nature of benevolence. Its author’s talent and insight are outstanding, and his learning is comprehensive; his understanding of principle is precise and pertinent, and his expression brims with vitality. Truly an exceptional scholar under Heaven! He fully deserves recommendation in first place in the Metropolitan Examination.

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Reader: The sage’s benevolence is one with Heaven. Most writers can state this, but their tedious generalities are tiresome. This composition bases its explanation on the spontaneous essential nature of benevolence and captures the fundamental meaning particularly well. Moreover, its arguments are precise and sound, its literary expression flourishes, its writing is vigorous, and its talent flows freely. Truly an extraordinary scholar! For recommendation in first place in the Metropolitan Examination, who but you?

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
考試官侍講學士尹批本仁體立說開闔千數百
言而矩矱不失盖老於為文者佳士佳士
考試官大學士李批以聖人仁政本於仁心立意
反覆議論無一長語可敬
聖人之道猶天然天生萬物而不已者仁而已
矣聖人體萬物而無外者亦仁而已矣夫仁者
何也天之理而人得之以為心者也聖人與天
下同得之故其心與天下為一其心與天下為
一故不能不兼體乎天下與天下為一者心也
===
出之以兼體乎天下者政也心以本之政以成
之而天下之物無復有外于聖人之仁者矣故
聖人之于天下其心若是之閔閔焉切也其政
若是之詳也而非聖人之有所強也聖人能全
是仁則其心之于天下不得不切其心切則其
政不得不詳而皆其得于天之不容已者也故
聖人如天之覆物而天下戴聖人之治亦如天
故聖人與天配也吾甞讀易而見天之道矣易
言乾元資始坤元資生則是始萬物者莫過于

translation_en:
Examiner Yin, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: The argument is grounded in the essential nature of benevolence. Through more than a thousand words, its development and closure never depart from proper standards. Surely this is someone seasoned in composition. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!

Examiner Li, Grand Secretary, comments: The central argument is that the sage’s benevolent government is rooted in his benevolent heart. It discusses this from every angle without a single superfluous word. Admirable.

The Way of the sage resembles Heaven. Yet what enables Heaven to generate the myriad things without ceasing is nothing other than benevolence; what enables the sage to embrace the myriad things as one body, excluding nothing, is likewise nothing other than benevolence. What, then, is benevolence? It is the principle of Heaven that human beings receive as their heart. The sage receives it in common with all under Heaven; therefore his heart is one with all under Heaven. Because his heart is one with all under Heaven, he cannot but embrace all under Heaven as one body. What is one with all under Heaven is his heart; what issues forth to embrace all under Heaven as one body is his government. His heart provides its foundation, and his government brings it to fulfillment, so that nothing in the world remains outside the sage’s benevolence.

Thus, in his relation to all under Heaven, the sage’s heart is so solicitous and deeply concerned, and his government so thorough; yet none of this involves any forcing on the sage’s part. Because the sage fully preserves this benevolence, his heart cannot but care deeply for all under Heaven. Because his heart cares deeply, his government cannot but be thorough. All of this proceeds irresistibly from what he has received from Heaven. Thus the sage is like Heaven sheltering all things, and all under Heaven revere the sage’s rule as they do Heaven. Hence the sage is Heaven’s counterpart.

I once read the Book of Changes and discerned the Way of Heaven. The Changes says, “From Qian’s primal power all things derive their beginning; from Kun’s primal power all things derive their birth.” This means that, in giving the myriad things their beginning, nothing surpasses …

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
乾生萬物者莫過于坤也吾以為造化盡于乾
坤矣及至于復而曰復其見天地之心乎夫易
不以乾坤為天地之心而繫之于復何也嗟乎
此可以識仁矣夫復者生氣之機天地不息之
化是乾坤之本也故其于乾也曰其靜也專其
動也直而大生焉其于坤也曰其靜也翕其動
也闢而廣生焉夫其靜之專矣而動即直靜之
翕矣而動即闢其機不可得而止者其端實始
于復故乾坤廣大之功人所共見而復幾微之
===
妙人不可得而知吾于是而歎天道之有本也
生者不得不生始者不得不始乾坤之所以為
廣大者也今夫日月之明星辰之列四時之行
雨霜露雷之殊山川之流峙此生理也萬物之
並育並長羣分類聚此生理也然自復而見焉
其機之不容已者也所謂仁體也故天無息機
而物亦無息天無外物而物亦無能外天者所
謂仁體也繼其善而性成焉賦之性而心生焉
是心者天地萬物之統也人得之以為生者也

punctuated: 乾，生萬物者莫過于坤也。吾以為造化盡于乾坤矣。及至于復，而曰：「復，其見天地之心乎！」夫易不以乾坤為天地之心，而繫之于復，何也？嗟乎！此可以識仁矣。夫復者，生氣之機，天地不息之化，是乾坤之本也。故其于乾也曰：「其靜也專，其動也直，而大生焉。」其于坤也曰：「其靜也翕，其動也闢，而廣生焉。」夫其靜之專矣，而動即直；靜之翕矣，而動即闢。其機不可得而止者，其端實始于復。故乾坤廣大之功，人所共見，而復幾微之妙，人不可得而知。吾于是而歎天道之有本也。生者不得不生，始者不得不始，乾坤之所以為廣大者也。今夫日月之明，星辰之列，四時之行，雨霜露雷之殊，山川之流峙，此生理也。萬物之並育並長，羣分類聚，此生理也。然自復而見焉，其機之不容已者也，所謂仁體也。故天無息機，而物亦無息；天無外物，而物亦無能外天者，所謂仁體也。繼其善而性成焉，賦之性而心生焉。是心者，天地萬物之統也，人得之以為生者也，
translation_en: …Qian; in giving life to the myriad things, nothing surpasses Kun. I had thought that the work of creation and transformation was exhausted by Qian and Kun. Yet when the Book of Changes reaches Fu (Return), it says: “In Return, do we not see the heart of Heaven and Earth!” Why does the Book of Changes locate the heart of Heaven and Earth in Return, rather than in Qian and Kun? Ah! Through this we may understand benevolence. Return is the incipient impulse of life-giving qi, the unceasing transformation of Heaven and Earth: it is the foundation of Qian and Kun. Thus, of Qian it says: “In stillness it is concentrated; in movement it is direct, and thereby it brings forth life on a great scale.” Of Kun it says: “In stillness it is closed; in movement it opens, and thereby it brings forth life far and wide.” Concentrated in stillness, it becomes direct as soon as it moves; closed in stillness, it opens as soon as it moves. This impulse, which cannot be halted, has its very inception in Return. Thus everyone sees the vast accomplishments of Qian and Kun, yet people cannot apprehend the subtle wonder of Return at its inception. At this I marvel that the Way of Heaven has a foundation. That which gives life cannot but give life; that which initiates cannot but initiate: this is what makes Qian and Kun so vast. Now, the brightness of sun and moon, the array of stars, the progress of the four seasons, the different manifestations of rain, frost, dew, and thunder, the flowing rivers and standing mountains—all are this principle of life. The myriad things, nourished and growing together, dividing into groups and gathering according to kind—all are this principle of life. Yet it is through Return that we see the impulse that cannot cease. This is what is called the substance of benevolence. Thus Heaven has no cessation in its generative impulse, and things likewise have no cessation; Heaven excludes no thing, and no thing can stand outside Heaven. This is what is called the substance of benevolence. In continuing its goodness, nature is fulfilled; through the endowment of that nature, the heart comes into being. This heart unites Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things; it is what human beings receive in order to live…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
所謂仁體也故聖人之心與萬物為一體而無
一物而不愛則亦無一物而在其所忍也故聖
人不能無不忍之心不能無不忍之心則不能
無不忍之政合心與政而聖人之仁始全此亦
其理本如是也吾嘗觀于聖人之政而見其制
為宮室以使民居若是之備也制耒耜教稼穡
耕鑿以使民飲食若是之周也制君臣父子上
下貴賤親疎內外之倫而別其禮若是之有秩
也制其器用車旗衣服之等若是之辨也嗟乎
===
聖人之政何其詳也然而未也慮其不明于相
生相養之道而爭以戕也而為之設吏以治之
慮其不明于性分而不能從上以治也而聯師
以教之又慮其不若于治不率于教也而刑以
齊之又懼其甚也而兵以威之嗟乎何其詳之
至也猶未已也服牛乘馬驅虎豹而遠之山林
川澤慮漁獵之不以時也而網罟之禁行焉所
以及物也方外之國治而不迫聽而不治而羈
縻之政行焉所以柔夷狄也嗟乎又何其益詳

translation_en:
…This is what is called the substance of benevolence. Thus the sage’s heart forms one body with the myriad things: there is nothing he does not love, and therefore nothing whose suffering he can bear. The sage therefore cannot lack a heart that cannot bear others’ suffering; possessing such a heart, he cannot fail to practice government that cannot bear their suffering. Only when heart and government are united is the sage’s benevolence complete. This, too, is simply how its underlying principle must be.

I have examined the sage’s government and seen how comprehensively he devised dwellings to house the people; how thoroughly he devised plows and plowshares and taught sowing and reaping, tilling fields and digging wells, so that the people might eat and drink; how orderly were the relationships he established between ruler and minister, father and son, superior and inferior, noble and lowly, close and distant kin, and those within and without, distinguishing the rites appropriate to each; and how clearly differentiated were the gradations he established for utensils, carriages and banners, and clothing. Ah! How detailed is the sage’s government! Yet this was not all. Fearing that people would not understand the way of sustaining and nourishing one another, but would contend and injure one another, he established officials to govern them. Fearing that they would not understand their innate endowments and proper duties, and thus could not follow their superiors in maintaining order, he organized teachers [?] to instruct them. Further fearing that they would not submit to government or follow its teachings, he used punishments to bring them into conformity. Fearing still more extreme misconduct, he used military force to overawe them. Ah! How utterly comprehensive it was!

Still he did not stop. He yoked oxen and rode horses, and drove tigers and leopards far away. In mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes, fearing that fishing and hunting would take place out of season, he enforced prohibitions on nets: this was how his care extended to other creatures. As for countries beyond his domain, he governed without coercion and attended to their affairs without administering them directly; he practiced a policy of loose rein, thereby conciliating the Yi and Di peoples. Ah! How much more comprehensive still…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
又何其繾綣委曲煩而不厭也其為之制也纖
悉而無不足也其慮也又何其勤也此聖人之
所不容已者也今夫人未有不愛其四肢百骸
者也故其擁護亦未有如四肢百骸者也慈母
未有不愛其赤子者也故其拊摩調適亦未有
如慈母之于赤子者也此其切于心而不容已
出于天而不自知者也聖人視天下之人其未
有寧居也若已之無所歸也故為之不容于不
備也聖人視天下之人其未得飲食之養也若
===
已之饑且渴也故其事不容于不周也聖人視
天下之人其彝倫之未正而等威之未别也若
已之紊于分義也故不容不辨且秩也其未治
也若已擾之其未得所教也若已罔之其兵刑
之未飭也若已慢令以致之其鳥獸蟲魚方外
之國一物之失其所也若已遺之惻惻然而圖
焉皇皇然而靡暇焉必如是而後其心始慰也
蓋聖人之心猶之天道之自復而見焉其機不
可已也聖人之達于政者之不可已猶之天之

punctuated: 又何其繾綣委曲，煩而不厭也！其為之制也，纖悉而無不足也；其慮也，又何其勤也！此聖人之所不容已者也。今夫人未有不愛其四肢百骸者也，故其擁護亦未有如四肢百骸者也。慈母未有不愛其赤子者也，故其拊摩調適亦未有如慈母之于赤子者也。此其切于心而不容已，出于天而不自知者也。聖人視天下之人，其未有寧居也，若已之無所歸也，故為之不容于不備也。聖人視天下之人，其未得飲食之養也，若已之饑且渴也，故其事不容于不周也。聖人視天下之人，其彝倫之未正而等威之未别也，若已之紊于分義也，故不容不辨且秩也。其未治也，若已擾之；其未得所教也，若已罔之；其兵刑之未飭也，若已慢令以致之；其鳥獸蟲魚、方外之國，一物之失其所也，若已遺之。惻惻然而圖焉，皇皇然而靡暇焉，必如是而後其心始慰也。蓋聖人之心，猶之天道之自復而見焉，其機不可已也。聖人之達于政者之不可已，猶之天之
translation_en:
…And how deeply solicitous and painstaking they were, never wearying of the trouble! The institutions they established were comprehensive in every detail, lacking nothing; how diligent, too, was their care! This is what the sages could not refrain from doing. Now, no one fails to cherish his own limbs and every part of his body; hence nothing receives such protection as these. No loving mother fails to cherish her infant; hence nothing compares with a loving mother's soothing care and adjustment to her infant's needs. These concerns press upon the heart and cannot be restrained; they arise from Heaven without conscious awareness.

When the sages saw people in the world without a peaceful dwelling, it was as though they themselves had nowhere to return; thus they could not but make complete provision for them. When the sages saw people in the world lacking the nourishment of food and drink, it was as though they themselves were hungry and thirsty; thus their efforts could not but be thorough. When the sages saw that people's enduring human relationships were not properly ordered and distinctions of rank and dignity were not clearly drawn, it was as though their own allotted duties and obligations were in disorder; thus they could not but distinguish and order them. When the people were not well governed, it was as though the sages themselves had disturbed them; when the people had not received appropriate instruction, it was as though the sages themselves had misled them. When military affairs and punishments were not properly regulated, it was as though their own laxity in issuing commands had brought this about. If any single creature among the birds, beasts, insects, and fish, or any country beyond the realm, failed to find its proper place, it was as though the sages themselves had neglected it. With aching concern they devised plans for these things; anxiously they labored, allowing themselves no leisure. Only by acting thus could their hearts at last find comfort.

For the heart of a sage is like the Way of Heaven, which manifests itself in its own returning: its animating impulse cannot cease. The irrepressible expression of the sage's heart in government is like Heaven's…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
資始資生莫不由是出也而日月星辰雨霜露
雷四時之序山川之有常萬物之聚散皆其不
可已者為之也是故聖人之道自居處食息之
微至于倫理等威之辨治教之綱刑罰兵律之
紀下及服乘之法網罟之禁羈縻之禮事之大
小不同而皆出于天然自有之則以覆冒天下
天下共由而不知也推之東海西海而準南海
北海而準盡天所覆之地無所不及天下亦共
由而不知也化溢中國施于蠻貊擊壤可封之
===
民相與安于內重譯欵關之使貢獒獻矢執玉
之人流沙海外星羅之國相與樂于外跂息蠕
動之物皆各得其所焉以戴聖人之覆而天下
亦共由而不知也經之萬世之遠前乎此者徵
焉後乎此者俟焉天有常覆聖人有常道天不
變聖人之道亦不變而天下亦共由而不知也
故聖人之覆天下也如天而天下之囿于聖人
之覆也如天之蕩蕩而不可名而治極矣此仁
之體也聖人與天下同得之者也人得之而失

之人流沙海外星羅之國相與樂于外跂息蠕
動之物皆各得其所焉以戴聖人之覆而天下
亦共由而不知也經之萬世之遠前乎此者徵

變聖人之道亦不變而天下亦共由而不知也
故聖人之覆天下也如天而天下之囿于聖人
之覆也如天之蕩蕩而不可名而治極矣此仁
之體也聖人與天下同得之者也人得之而失
punctuated: 資始資生，莫不由是出也。而日月星辰、雨霜露雷、四時之序、山川之有常、萬物之聚散，皆其不可已者為之也。是故聖人之道，自居處食息之微，至于倫理等威之辨、治教之綱、刑罰兵律之紀，下及服乘之法、網罟之禁、羈縻之禮，事之大小不同，而皆出于天然自有之則，以覆冒天下，天下共由而不知也。推之東海西海而準，南海北海而準，盡天所覆之地，無所不及，天下亦共由而不知也。化溢中國，施于蠻貊，擊壤可封之民相與安于內；重譯欵關之使、貢獒獻矢執玉之人、流沙海外星羅之國，相與樂于外；跂息蠕動之物，皆各得其所焉，以戴聖人之覆，而天下亦共由而不知也。經之萬世之遠，前乎此者徵焉，後乎此者俟焉。天有常覆，聖人有常道，天不變，聖人之道亦不變，而天下亦共由而不知也。故聖人之覆天下也如天，而天下之囿于聖人之覆也，如天之蕩蕩而不可名，而治極矣。此仁之體也，聖人與天下同得之者也。人得之而失
translation_en:
…providing the source of all beginnings and of all life: none of this fails to issue from this principle. The sun, moon, and stars; rain, frost, dew, and thunder; the succession of the four seasons; the constancy of mountains and rivers; and the gathering and dispersal of all things—all are brought about by its ceaseless activity. Thus the Way of the sage extends from the minutiae of dwelling, eating, and resting to the distinctions of human relationships and degrees of rank and dignity, the guiding principles of government and instruction, and the rules of punishment and military discipline. It reaches down to regulations for clothing and conveyances, prohibitions concerning nets and snares, and the rites for maintaining loose control over distant peoples. These matters differ in magnitude, yet all issue from principles inherently present in nature, thereby encompassing and sheltering all under Heaven. All under Heaven follow them together without knowing it. Extended to the eastern and western seas, they hold true; to the southern and northern seas, they hold true. Throughout the lands covered by Heaven, there is nowhere they do not reach, and all under Heaven likewise follow them together without knowing it.

The sage’s transforming influence overflows the Central Realm and extends to the Man and Mo peoples. Within, the people who play at striking clods, each worthy of receiving a fief, live together in peace. Beyond, envoys who pass through successive interpreters and present themselves at the frontier gates, people who offer mastiffs and arrows as tribute or bear jade tokens of audience, and states scattered like stars in the lands of the Flowing Sands and beyond the seas all rejoice together. Creatures that stand on tiptoe, breathe, or crawl each find their proper place and enjoy the sage’s shelter. Yet all under Heaven likewise follow it together without knowing it.

Across the vast span of ten thousand generations, those who came before furnish its verification, and those yet to come may be awaited to confirm it. Heaven has its constant sheltering power; the sage has his constant Way. Heaven does not change, nor does the sage’s Way, and all under Heaven likewise follow it together without knowing it. Thus the sage shelters all under Heaven as Heaven does. All under Heaven dwell within the sage’s shelter, which, like Heaven in its boundless vastness, cannot be adequately named; government thereby reaches its utmost perfection. This is the substance of benevolence, something the sage and all others under Heaven alike receive. Other people receive it but lose…

translation_en:
…it, whereas the sage obtains it and preserves it whole. Although people lose it, their principle of life cannot lie outside it; when the sage preserves it whole, this is precisely the same principle of life shared by all. Thus the sage gives expression to what they share, and none under Heaven can stand outside what they originally have in common. There is no coercion in this. This is what is meant by benevolence sheltering all under Heaven.
Memorial
A model memorial of thanks for the imperial composition “Further Verses on Concern for Farmers,” bestowed upon the grand secretaries and other officials for them to compose matching verses.
By Ge Lun.
Comment by Associate Examiner Fang, Acting Bureau Director: The form is dignified and the phrasing ornate and beautiful. An outstanding example of four-and-six-character parallel prose; select it for inclusion.
Comment by Associate Examiner Lü, Compiler: It successfully extols Our Emperor’s filial devotion in carrying forward his predecessor’s aspirations and his benevolence in showing compassion for farmers. Its earnest loyalty and devoted wishes reveal themselves naturally. It is classically elegant and beautiful, with a fitting form.
Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Senior Compiler: Its praise is fittingly expressed. Evidently the writer has been steeped in Our Emperor’s transforming influence of benevolence and filial devotion and has deeply apprehended it. Moreover, it conforms to classical standards while remaining beautiful, and is deeply earnest yet polished. An excellent memorial; it should be included as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Dong, Right Adviser to the Heir Apparent: Its language and meaning are classically elegant. Evidently it has captured something of the legacy of the “Airs of Bin” and the “Hymns of Zhou.” Its intent is deeply felt and its emotions sincere; it gives an almost exhaustive portrayal of Our Emperor’s utmost concern for benevolence and filial devotion. It merits inclusion.

translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Yin, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: “The thought is profound and the language graceful. It extols Our Emperor’s abundant benevolence and filial devotion in a manner beyond the reach of ordinary scholars. It should be recorded as a model.”
Comment by Examiner Li, Grand Secretary: “Sincere loyalty and gratitude appear in the praise.”
On a certain day of a certain month in a certain year of Jiajing, we humbly received the favor of His Majesty’s composing, at the Pavilion for Inspecting Agriculture, the imperially composed poem Further Thoughts on Agriculture, and bestowing it upon us, his servants, to compose poems in response.
Spring brings harmony throughout the Four Seas; nurturing in response [?], he takes thought for the work of farming. Within the Ninefold Palace, enjoying timely repose, he sets forth words whose brilliance rivals the seven luminaries. Their meaning accords with the poems of Bin; their Way exalts the songs of Yu. Truly, it is a sage who can compose such works; looking up to the emperor’s virtue, we find it beyond naming. Together we receive his dragon-adorned composition, charged, as attendants close to the throne, with composing continuations. All alike receive his great beneficence, rejoicing that it extends everywhere among the common people. We, your servants, in utmost joy and delight, bow our heads to the ground and kowtow, submitting these words:
We humbly consider that Shennong, the Divine Farmer, established the supreme standard and first introduced the plow and plowshare; Hou Ji, honored with sacrifices alongside Heaven, broadly inaugurated instruction in tilling and weeding. Though the age was peaceful, concern for those suffering hunger or drowning prompted daily diligence; wearing humble garments and going out to the fields brought peace [?], with the heart ever reverent and watchful. For the Way transmitted from emperor to emperor and king to king is the foundation of their great undertaking; and the bond through which ruler and ministers form one body, in a flourishing age …

punctuated: 斯見，允稱迪哲，永介洪庥。慨千畝之籍不修，邈三代之隆莫繼。丕啓雍熈之運，實惟堯舜之君。兹盖伏遇皇帝陛下，至仁覆物，大孝尊親，中和收位育之功，制作闡聖神之秘。憂先天下，深知稼穡之艱；食後日中，兼採芻蕘之見。兹屬楓宸之多暇，睠惟穀雨之届期，翠華戾止于帝田，清蹕暫紆乎畯舍。爰念憫農舊詠，雖詞出乎古人；繹思詒訓當年，嘗面承于皇考。淵衷妙啓，麗藻重輝，即一句以發端，各聯奎璧
translation_en:
…is here revealed. Truly this may be called enlightened wisdom, securing lasting and abundant blessings. We lament that the thousand-mu imperial ploughing field has fallen into neglect and that the distant grandeur of the Three Dynasties has found no successor. To inaugurate a great age of harmony and prosperity requires indeed a ruler like Yao or Shun.
Now we humbly behold Your Majesty the Emperor: your consummate benevolence shelters all beings, and your profound filial devotion honors your parents. Through equilibrium and harmony, you bring all things to their proper places and nurture their growth; through institutions and rites, you reveal the mysteries of sagely and divine wisdom. You take thought for the realm before all others, knowing deeply the hardships of sowing and reaping; you delay your meal until after midday, also seeking the views of grass cutters and wood gatherers.
Now, with leisure amid your palace duties, and mindful that the Grain Rain season had arrived, your kingfisher-feather standard came to the imperial fields, and your procession, its way cleared, briefly turned toward the field overseer’s dwelling. You recalled the old verses on the hardships of farmers: though their words came from an ancient poet, reflecting upon the year when that instruction was imparted, you had received it face to face from your late imperial father. Subtle inspiration arose from your profound heart, and splendid verse shone anew. Taking a single line as the opening, you strung together, in each composition, the stars of Kui and Bi, emblems of literary brilliance…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
成四詩而諧韻並燦珠璣備述老農之苦
辛切戒牧民之朘削同我婦子宛然依媚

…forming four poems in harmonious rhyme, all brilliant as pearls and gems. They fully recount the hardships of old farmers and sternly warn those who govern the people against their impoverishment through exactions. “Together with our wives and children”: these are truly words of affection and attachment. Looking upon the food on the platter, they are indeed a prayer for abundant harvests. Envisioning ample provision for public and private needs alike, they anticipate blessings spreading everywhere [?]; declaring that the people's suffering must be understood, they particularly rebuke brutality and boorishness. Earnest admonitions recur, their words expressing true feeling; meticulous and comprehensive, they reveal deep concern and far-reaching foresight. Composed by Your Majesty at the place where you inspected farming, the poems were bestowed equally upon your attendant officials. In wonder we behold the brilliance of your precious calligraphy, descending from Heaven; in reverence we hear your august words proclaimed, reaching every place. To compose worthy responses is difficult; the honor we receive is beyond measure.
We, your servants, unworthily hold offices of confidential service and posts charged with assisting you. Consuming generous stipends to no purpose, how could we forget, as we eat and drink, the sovereign's beneficence? Possessing only simple loyalty, we contribute nothing to Heaven's work of harmonizing the world. Undeservedly receiving these gifts of precious jade, we are ashamed to lack fine gems to offer in return. Drinking from the rivers, each of us knows contentment; how could we contain our personal joy and grateful devotion? Those who have studied at the sage's gate find it difficult to speak: we cannot adequately express the excellence of what we praise.

…you will know what you may expect of yourself.
Examiner Grand Secretary Li comments: The edicts and commands of our two founding ancestors and His Majesty have been clearly proclaimed throughout the realm; everyone surely knows them with reverence. Yet their benevolent intent may not always have been duly disseminated and fully put into effect. This is indeed the fault of the responsible officials. This composition deeply grasps that intent and, moreover, expounds it fully and in detail. I select it for inclusion.
Heaven accomplishes its great work of transformation through yin and yang; what breathes forth and stirs their vital energies, causing the myriad things to rise into ceaseless activity, is wind. The sage conducts great affairs of government through benevolence and righteousness; what disseminates his intentions, causing the myriad people to respond with tireless enthusiasm, is his commands. If Heaven did not act upon the myriad things through wind, the vital energies of yin and yang would stagnate rather than circulate; those things stirred to activity would collapse, and the great work of transformation might well be obstructed. If the sage did not promulgate his commands among the myriad people, the Way of benevolence and righteousness would remain obscure rather than manifest; those stirred to enthusiasm would grow idle, and great affairs of government might well be impeded.
The Book of Changes says: “Of the things that move the myriad things, none is swifter than wind.” This means that, when the myriad things receive the wind, yin and yang become harmonious and circulate freely: this is how Heaven accomplishes its great work of transformation. The Book of Documents says: “The sovereign standard’s promulgated words are constant norms and instructions.” This means that, when the myriad people receive commands, benevolence and righteousness are clearly disseminated: this is how the sage conducts great affairs of government. 盖昔者聖人象天之風以施命令，故在《易》，申命、渙號、施誥四方之文，必繫之巽體之卦。《書》曰：「令出惟行，弗惟反。」《傳》曰：「國之安危在出令。」又曰：「令重則君尊。」故善觀人國者，即其令之張弛，知其勢之盛衰；審其令之通塞，知其政之美疵。盖政出於命令，自古所爲重也。
稽古唐虞，命官咨治，諄諄訓戒，不越乎事天理民之事。其時君臣都俞一堂之上，未有命令，而命令之出所繇始也。故九官十二牧率其常職，以後先翊戴，昭熈治績於久遠。上哉邈乎，非後代之可及已！降及三代，命令始作，行之征伐，施之告戒，其辭寢以
translation_en:
…the promulgation of edicts and commands by our Two Founding Ancestors and our reigning Emperor, from which the great policies of this dynasty proceed. You wish those trained in learning to reflect upon their meaning and, by extension, examine the texts of the Canons, Counsels, Instructions, and Oaths, together with the edicts and commands of the Han rulers, setting these matters clearly forth in writing [?]. Ignorant as I am, how could I adequately understand them? Nevertheless, I dare not fail to present a brief account.
In former times, the sages modeled themselves upon Heaven’s wind in issuing commands. Thus, in the Book of Changes, passages concerning the reiteration of commands, the dispersal of proclamations, and the issuing of announcements to the four quarters are invariably attached to hexagrams containing the trigram Xun, Wind. The Book of Documents says: “Once a command is issued, it must be carried out, not reversed.” The Commentary says: “The security or peril of a state depends upon the issuing of commands.” It also says: “When commands carry weight, the ruler is honored.” Thus, those skilled in assessing a state can discern the rise or decline of its power from the rigor or laxity of its commands; by examining whether its commands pass freely or encounter obstruction, they can discern the merits or defects of its government. Government proceeds from commands: this is why they have been regarded as weighty since antiquity.
Examining the ancient ages of Tang and Yu, we find that officials were appointed and counsel sought on government, with earnest instructions and admonitions concerning nothing beyond serving Heaven and governing the people. At that time, ruler and ministers exchanged words of approval in a single hall. Formal commands did not yet exist, but here lay the origin of their issuance. Thus the nine officials and twelve regional governors followed their regular duties, assisting and supporting their rulers in succession, and made the achievements of government shine through distant ages. How exalted and remote! Later ages could not attain their heights. title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
詳矣是故夏有甘誓胤征之文商有湯誓
湯誥之文周之誓誥多申於弔伐之際其
言反覆周備忠厚而嚴至其制則士師掌
五戒以先後刑罰勿使罪麗於民自誓誥
以下各有所用其化行於族閭州黨之間
百世記之可思也夫自唐虞至周上下千
數百年雖命令之施不能不因乎時然仁
義兼施時出而不悖則二帝三王之所同
也乃若其文之殊則楊雄所稱渾渾之書
===
固不得與灝灝噩噩者作也周道衰而王
迹熄秦苛熾而德化蕩漢承其敝政教雖
不純於仁義然取往善鑒近失詔令所布
不無一二庶幾乎古者獨惜乎其不皆然
耳是故告諭諸將約法三章雖足慰秦父
兄願戴之心矣而不事詩書馬上之習未
滌也議法求言佐農養老雖能動山東癃
老扶杖之聽矣而不遑禮樂伯世之治猶

…became more detailed. Thus, under the Xia there were the texts “The Oath at Gan” and “The Expedition of Yin”; under the Shang, “The Oath of Tang” and “The Announcement of Tang.” The oaths and announcements of the Zhou were mostly proclaimed on occasions of relieving the afflicted and conducting punitive campaigns. Their language was reiterative and comprehensive, generous and sincere, yet stern. As for their institutions, the Judicial Officers administered the five admonitions, placing them before and after penal measures so that the people would not incur guilt. Oaths, announcements, and the other forms each had their respective uses, and their transforming influence spread among the clan and neighborhood units. Remembered for a hundred generations, these practices merit reflection.
From Tang and Yu down to the Zhou, a span of well over a thousand years, the application of commands and ordinances necessarily varied with the times. Yet the joint exercise of benevolence and righteousness, issuing commands at the appropriate time without departing from these principles, was common to the Two Emperors and Three Kings. As for differences in their writing, however, the documents that Yang Xiong called “deep and all-embracing” certainly could not be placed alongside [?] those he called “vast and expansive” and “grave and direct.”
The Way of Zhou declined, and the achievements of the true kings faded away; Qin’s harshness intensified, and moral transformation was swept aside. The Han inherited these abuses. Although its government and instruction were not grounded wholly in benevolence and righteousness, it adopted what had been good in the past and took warning from recent failures. Among the edicts and ordinances it promulgated, there were indeed one or two that approached those of antiquity. One can only regret that they were not all so.
Thus, admonishing the generals and reducing the laws to three articles sufficed to comfort the elders of Qin in their desire to support their ruler; yet he did not devote himself to the Odes and Documents, and his habits of ruling from horseback remained unpurged. Deliberating on laws, soliciting advice, assisting agriculture, and supporting the elderly could indeed stir the infirm elders east of the passes as they leaned on their staffs to listen; yet he found no leisure for rites and music, and still followed the governmental practices of an age of hegemons. As for instituting the recommendation of the Filial and Incorrupt and sending Erudites on inspection tours, Emperor Wu…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
宣之詔令雖稍稍可觀而其虛耗嚴刻之
政已遠於高文寬仁恭儉之風矣亦何論
其他也哉東都再起建武之規摹永平之
治績爛然條貫可睹即之西京閎大弘遠
之畧然當是時皆出之以實意御史大夫
下相國相國下諸侯王御史中執法下郡
守次第舉行務稱明德詔令非虛施也故
隋王通取漢七制之文列為四範以續四
經非以其猶近古耶而其得失尚不免後
===
人之論則魏晉以後所載駁乎無取於仁
義者抑何以指議為哉洪惟我
太祖高皇帝聖神文武膺
天眷命驅掃胡氛廓清華夏心切黔黎慮周海
宇
諭左右丞相御史大夫布政叅政則有詔
戒有司責任禁諸司姦貪擾民則有詔
封元後諭西南諸夷則有詔定神祇以明祀
開科舉以求賢則又有詔他如爵賞功臣

宣之詔令雖稍稍可觀，而其虛耗嚴刻之政，已遠於高文寬仁恭儉之風矣，亦何論其他也哉！東都再起，建武之規摹、永平之治績，爛然條貫可睹，即之西京閎大弘遠之畧。然當是時，皆出之以實意，御史大夫下相國，相國下諸侯王，御史中執法下郡守，次第舉行，務稱明德，詔令非虛施也。故隋王通取漢七制之文，列為四範，以續四經，非以其猶近古耶？而其得失尚不免後人之論，則魏晉以後所載駁乎無取於仁義者，抑何以指議為哉！
洪惟我太祖高皇帝，聖神文武，膺天眷命，驅掃胡氛，廓清華夏，心切黔黎，慮周海宇。諭左右丞相、御史大夫、布政、叅政，則有詔；戒有司責任、禁諸司姦貪擾民，則有詔；封元後、諭西南諸夷，則有詔；定神祇以明祀、開科舉以求賢，則又有詔。他如爵賞功臣
translation_en:
…Although the edicts of Emperors Wu and Xuan had some merit, their policies, which depleted resources and imposed harsh rule, had already departed far from the generous, humane, reverent, and frugal spirit of Emperors Gao and Wen. What need is there to discuss the others? When the dynasty rose again at the Eastern Capital, the institutional plans of the Jianwu era and the achievements in government of the Yongping era displayed a brilliant and discernible order, approaching the broad and far-reaching strategies of the Western Capital. At that time, however, all these measures proceeded from sincere intent. The Censor-in-Chief transmitted orders to the Chancellor of State; the Chancellor of State transmitted them to the enfeoffed kings; and the censorial law-enforcement officials transmitted them to the commandery governors. They were implemented in due sequence, with every effort to accord with the ruler’s illustrious virtue: edicts were not issued in vain. Thus Wang Tong of the Sui selected writings from seven Han reigns and arranged them into Four Models, to continue the Four Classics. Was this not because they still stood close to antiquity? Yet even their successes and failures could not escape the judgment of later generations. As for the heterogeneous writings recorded from the Wei and Jin onward, which drew nothing from benevolence and righteousness, what purpose would there be in singling them out for criticism?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, sagely and divine, accomplished in civil and military affairs, received Heaven’s gracious mandate, swept away the barbarian menace, and cleared the Chinese realm. His heart was deeply concerned for the common people, and his care encompassed all within the seas. There were edicts instructing the Chief Councilors of the Left and Right, the Censor-in-Chief, the Provincial Administration Commissioners, and the Administration Vice Commissioners; edicts admonishing the responsible officials to fulfill their duties and forbidding the various offices from troubling the people through corruption and greed; edicts investing the principal empress and instructing the various non-Chinese peoples of the southwest; and further edicts establishing the proper standing of the spirits of heaven and earth to clarify sacrificial worship, and inaugurating the civil-service examinations to seek worthy men. Other measures included granting titles and rewards to meritorious officials…

text:
慰撫軍士勸農桑興學校尊齒德恤孤獨
正禮儀風俗以明教因星變雷威而飭戒
其炳炳大者固難以更僕數也典謨訓誓
之文何以過之啓萬年無疆之祚盖有所
從出矣我
成祖文皇帝受
命穆清同符
聖祖掃蕩沙漠驅匪茹之深患
考卜燕京定不拔之洪基是故
===
詔令之大者曰封建曰冊立曰賜租曰恤獄
曰巡幸曰親征曰文武羣臣修職
綸音頒布無慮數十中外既遵由之以成化
矣今觀
訓言所載有稱創業難守成不易為君難為
臣不易矻矻於君臣交儆以成天下之治
理誨迪臣民委曲至千百言不置虞廷命
官咨治之勤何其異世一揆也我
皇上敬

慰撫軍士，勸農桑，興學校，尊齒德，恤孤獨，正禮儀風俗以明教，因星變雷威而飭戒，其炳炳大者，固難以更僕數也。典謨訓誓之文，何以過之？啓萬年無疆之祚，盖有所從出矣。
我成祖文皇帝受命穆清，同符聖祖，掃蕩沙漠，驅匪茹之深患，考卜燕京，定不拔之洪基。是故詔令之大者，曰封建，曰冊立，曰賜租，曰恤獄，曰巡幸，曰親征，曰文武羣臣修職。綸音頒布，無慮數十，中外既遵由之以成化矣。今觀訓言所載，有稱「創業難，守成不易；為君難，為臣不易」，矻矻於君臣交儆，以成天下之治理。誨迪臣民，委曲至千百言不置。虞廷命官咨治之勤，何其異世一揆也！
我皇上敬
translation_en:
…comforting and reassuring the soldiers, encouraging farming and sericulture, establishing schools, honoring age and virtue, caring for orphans and the solitary, rectifying ritual observances and customs to make moral instruction clear, and issuing admonitions in response to celestial anomalies and the awe-inspiring power of thunder: even these conspicuously great examples could scarcely be enumerated through successive changes of attendants. How could the Canons, Counsels, Instructions, and Oaths of the Book of Documents surpass these writings? The inauguration of an enduring imperial blessing, boundless for ten thousand years, surely had its source in these acts.
Our Emperor Chengzu Wen received the mandate in august purity and fulfilled the same auspicious signs as the Sagely Founder. He swept through the deserts, dispelled the grave menace of ruthless foes, examined and divined the suitability of Yanjing, and established a grand, unshakable foundation there. Thus, the principal subjects of his edicts were the enfeoffment of princes, formal investitures, grants of tax revenue [?], compassionate review of criminal cases, imperial tours, campaigns led by the emperor in person, and the diligent discharge of duties by all civil and military officials. Several dozen imperial pronouncements were promulgated, and those at court and beyond followed them to bring about moral transformation. Now, examining the admonitions recorded there, we find such statements as: “Founding a dynasty is difficult; preserving its achievements is not easy. Being a ruler is difficult; being a minister is not easy.” He labored tirelessly to have ruler and ministers admonish one another, thereby bringing orderly government to the realm. He instructed and guided his ministers and people, explaining matters fully in hundreds and thousands of words without cease. How closely his diligence matched that of the court of Yu in appointing officials and consulting on government—the same principles across different ages!

祖修治弘敷化理飭舉廢墜自
即位以至于今政務之大者昭宣於
詔勅所頒降備矣是故自
德教所推行言之則

親有問彝言所示天下莫不興孝敬焉
敬一有箴五箴有註誨諭所右天下莫不𨗳理
道焉自威刑所振敭言之則姦逆有誅不

赦宥廣推刑不過乎德矣叛命有征不終絕
其自新
恩施周流威不克乎愛矣以禮制之裁定言之

天勤民，法祖修治，弘敷化理，飭舉廢墜。自即位以至于今，政務之大者，昭宣於詔勅所頒降備矣。
是故自德教所推行言之，則明倫有典，饗親有問，彝言所示，天下莫不興孝敬焉。敬一有箴，五箴有註，誨諭所右，天下莫不𨗳理道焉。

以禮制之裁定言之，郊澤復皇祖之初儀，耕蠶重先王之本業，大享大祫之必按乎往制，尊
translation_en:
…Heaven and diligently caring for the people, following the ancestors in cultivating good government, broadly extending moral transformation and orderly rule, and restoring neglected institutions. From his accession to the present, all the great affairs of government have been fully and clearly proclaimed in the edicts and commands he has issued.
Thus, concerning the propagation of moral instruction, there is a canon elucidating human relationships and an inquiry concerning sacrificial offerings to parents [?]. Through the guidance of these enduring pronouncements, everyone throughout the realm is stirred to filial devotion and reverence. There is the Admonition on Reverent Unity (Jingyi), and there are annotations to the Five Admonitions. Through what these instructions uphold [?], everyone throughout the realm is guided along the Way of proper order.
Concerning the exercise of awe-inspiring punishment, traitors and rebels are executed, but investigations and punishments are not extended relentlessly to those who are innocent. Pardons and clemency are widely granted, so punishment does not exceed virtue. Those who defy commands are subjected to punitive expeditions, but their opportunity to reform is not permanently cut off. Gracious benefits circulate everywhere, so severity does not prevail over loving care.
Concerning the determination of ritual institutions, the suburban and marsh sacrifices to Heaven and Earth restore the original rites of the imperial ancestor. Ritual plowing and sericulture emphasize the fundamental occupations valued by the former kings. title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
天尊
祖之首正乎徽名百代曠儀於是乎其悉舉也
以紀綱之飭修言之官爵革冒濫之弊居
服嚴品式之辨
權綱總攬於獨斷職業稽勤於衆任百司常守
於是乎其咸一也其他若
大儀之播告
大慶之覃恩或值變而謹修省或遇災而肆寬
恤仁義之政不使有一夫之不被受焉故
渙汗所及亦如風之噓拂萬物而作奮其
氣薄海內外無幽遐之不達者矣夫有平
章協和包含溥博之度故其澤融液周徧
蟠際天地而無外有懷柔震疊陳常求懿

有憂勤惕厲艱難抑畏之思故其政慎始
圖終悠久而益章有制節謹度正大忠厚
之意故其習安儉守讓檢束而不蕩惇禮
樂尚寬和如膏粱之養生也故其施之惇

章協和包含溥博之度故其澤融液周徧
蟠際天地而無外有懷柔震疊陳常求懿
之志故其化光顯赫奕昭揭日月而莫踰
有憂勤惕厲艱難抑畏之思故其政愼始
圖終悠久而益章有制節謹度正大忠厚
之意故其習安儉守讓檢束而不蕩惇禮
樂尚寛和如膏粱之養生也故其施之惇
punctuated:
天尊祖之首正乎徽名，百代曠儀，於是乎其悉舉也。
以紀綱之飭修言之，官爵革冒濫之弊，居服嚴品式之辨，權綱總攬於獨斷，職業稽勤於衆任，百司常守，於是乎其咸一也。
其他若大儀之播告，大慶之覃恩，或值變而謹修省，或遇災而肆寬恤，仁義之政，不使有一夫之不被受焉。故渙汗所及，亦如風之噓拂萬物而作奮其氣，薄海內外，無幽遐之不達者矣。
夫有平章協和、包含溥博之度，故其澤融液周徧，蟠際天地而無外；有懷柔震疊、陳常求懿之志，故其化光顯赫奕，昭揭日月而莫踰；有憂勤惕厲、艱難抑畏之思，故其政慎始圖終，悠久而益章；有制節謹度、正大忠厚之意，故其習安儉守讓，檢束而不蕩。惇禮樂，尚寬和，如膏粱之養生也，故其施之惇
translation_en:
…Heaven and honoring the ancestors, giving first place to rectifying their august titles [?]. Ceremonies left unperformed for a hundred generations have thus all been carried out.
As for putting the governing order into good repair, abuses involving fraudulent and excessive grants of office and rank have been abolished, and distinctions prescribed by rank for dwellings and dress have been strictly enforced. The sovereign gathers the reins of authority into his own hands and decides independently; diligence in official duties is assessed among all those entrusted with responsibilities. The standing observances of the many offices have thus all been brought into conformity.
Other measures include proclamations of great ceremonies and the extension of imperial favor on occasions of great rejoicing. Sometimes extraordinary occurrences prompt earnest self-cultivation and reflection; sometimes disasters prompt generous clemency and relief. Under this government of benevolence and righteousness, not a single person is left without its benefits. Thus, wherever the imperial pronouncements reach, they are like the wind breathing over the myriad things and stirring their vital energies. Throughout the realm and beyond its seas, no place is too secluded or remote for them to reach.
Because he possesses the capacity to bring order and harmony, embracing all with breadth and generosity, his beneficence permeates everywhere, extending to the utmost bounds of Heaven and Earth and leaving nothing outside it. Because he is resolved to cherish and conciliate, to awe and subdue, to establish enduring norms and seek excellence, his transforming influence shines brilliantly, as conspicuous as the sun and moon, with nothing surpassing it. Because his thoughts dwell upon anxious diligence, vigilance, hardship, humility, and reverence, his government takes care at the beginning and plans for the end, becoming ever more illustrious as it endures. Because his intentions are governed by restraint and careful observance of proper measures, uprightness, loyalty, and generosity, the customs he fosters find contentment in frugality and uphold deference, remaining disciplined rather than unrestrained. He gives weight to ritual and music and esteems leniency and harmony, just as rich food and fine grain nourish life; hence, what he bestows is generous…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
大而成裕敕刑罰振剛嚴如藥石之伐病
也故其出之明作而有功蓋我
皇上仁義兼施之效行之家邦施之臣民歷三
紀于茲其大者無一不出之
命令焉宜其響傳者徯應逖聽者格化治功昭
輝光於四海理澤周流浹於萬世非往代
所可及焉然
德教雖推行矣所與承宣者或不無泥格之
患威刑雖振遏矣所與典訖者或未得制
===
中之理禮文裁定矣而揖讓之化難洽紀
綱修飭矣而防維之道罔周夫
聖人在上百司仰承
休德宜厲惕日夜以究事功而可以怠佚自曠
負職業之修舉哉故愚以為今日內外臣
工欲攄忠棐之忱以盡輔理之實必也幽
隱不欺若仰日月之明不敢蔽容光於照
臨也纖微必慎若畏雷霆之察不敢忘敬
心於戲豫也練習講圖反觀內究有一念

也故其出之明作而有功盖我

命令焉宜其響傳者傒應遡聽者格化治功昭
燀光於四海理澤周流浹於萬世非往代

患威刑雖振揚矣所與典詑者或未得制

綱修飭矣而防維之道罔周夫
===
聖人在上百司仰承
休德宜厲惕日夜以究事功而可以怠佚自曠
負職業之修舉哉故愚以為今日内外臣
工欲攄忠藎之忱以盡輔理之實必也幽
隱不欺若仰日月之明不敢蔽容光於照
臨也纖微必慎若畏雷霆之察不敢忘敬
恐於戲豫也練習講圖反觀内究有一念
punctuated:
大而成裕。敕刑罰，振剛嚴，如藥石之伐病也，故其出之明作而有功。蓋我皇上仁義兼施之效，行之家邦，施之臣民，歷三紀于茲，其大者無一不出之命令焉。宜其響傳者徯應，逖聽者格化，治功昭輝光於四海，理澤周流浹於萬世，非往代所可及焉。
然德教雖推行矣，所與承宣者或不無泥格之患；威刑雖振遏矣，所與典訖者或未得制中之理。禮文裁定矣，而揖讓之化難洽；紀綱修飭矣，而防維之道罔周。夫聖人在上，百司仰承休德，宜厲惕日夜，以究事功，而可以怠佚自曠，負職業之修舉哉？故愚以為今日內外臣工，欲攄忠棐之忱，以盡輔理之實，必也幽隱不欺，若仰日月之明，不敢蔽容光於照臨也；纖微必慎，若畏雷霆之察，不敢忘敬心於戲豫也。練習講圖，反觀內究，有一念
translation_en:
…ample and productive of abundance. He orders punishments and asserts stern authority, as medicines and mineral remedies attack disease; thus, when he applies them, they are discerningly administered and achieve results. Such are the effects of our Emperor’s combined exercise of benevolence and righteousness, practiced throughout his realm and extended to his officials and people for three twelve-year cycles now. Every major measure has issued through his commands. Fittingly, those to whom their sound is transmitted await them and respond, while those who hear them from afar are reached and transformed. The achievements of his government shine throughout the Four Seas, and the blessings of his rule circulate everywhere, benefiting ten thousand generations. Past ages could not match this.
Yet although moral instruction has been propagated, those entrusted with receiving and promulgating it may still obstruct its progress. Although the majesty of punishment has been asserted to restrain wrongdoing, those entrusted with its administration [?] may not yet have grasped the principle of achieving due balance. Ritual forms have been determined, yet the transforming influence of courtesy and deference has difficulty spreading everywhere. The governing framework has been put in order, yet its safeguards remain incomplete. With the sage above, the officials of every office look up to receive his beneficent virtue. They ought to remain vigilant day and night, bringing their work to fruition. How can they allow themselves to neglect their duties through indolence and ease, failing to discharge the responsibilities of their offices? Thus, in my humble view, if officials serving within and beyond the capital today wish to express their sincere loyalty and support, and fully perform the actual work of assisting government, they must practice no deception even in secret, as though looking up at the brightness of the sun and moon, not daring to screen even the smallest crevice from their illumination. They must be cautious in the slightest matters, as though fearing the scrutiny of thunder, not daring to forget reverence amid amusement and pleasure. They must train themselves, deliberate and plan, turn their gaze upon themselves and examine within. If there is a single thought…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
一事之合於
上心者必循循以勉之期竭其力之所致而始
終之不渝有一念一事之拂於
上令者必恇恇以戒之期止其心之所萌而肆
縱之必戒上之德澤使之下流民之疾苦
使之上達厲天下之士使修其行居天下
之民使安其業近者使之親附遠者使之
賓服方外之擾薄伐不試海內之氣清和
咸理休徵協而嘉祥集福履應而災變消
===
則易所謂言出乎身加乎民筦子所謂令
行若流水以宣播
上德沛流下澤雖風之疾行善入動萬物而不
止不足以喻其效矣此豈非內外臣工輔
理承化者之責哉詩曰嗟爾君子無恒安
處靖共爾位正直是與敢以為今之在位
者告民之質矣日用飲食群黎百姓徧為
爾德敢以為
太平盛治無疆頌焉

終之不渝有一念一事之拂於

賓服方外之擾薄伐不試海內之氣清和
咸理休徵協而嘉祥集福履應而災變消
則易所謂言出乎身加乎民莞子所謂令
行若流水以宣播
上德沛流下澤雖風之疾行善入動萬物而不
止不足以喻其效矣此豈非內外臣工輔
理承化者之責哉詩曰嗟爾君子無恒安
處靖共爾位正直是與敢以為今之在位
者告民之質矣日用飲食群黎百姓徧為
爾德敢以為
太平盛治無疆頌焉
punctuated: 一事之合於上心者，必循循以勉之，期竭其力之所致，而始終之不渝；有一念一事之拂於上令者，必恇恇以戒之，期止其心之所萌，而肆縱之必戒。上之德澤，使之下流；民之疾苦，使之上達。厲天下之士，使修其行；居天下之民，使安其業。近者使之親附，遠者使之賓服。方外之擾，薄伐不試；海內之氣，清和咸理。休徵協而嘉祥集，福履應而災變消。則《易》所謂「言出乎身，加乎民」，《筦子》所謂「令行若流水」，以宣播上德，沛流下澤。雖風之疾行善入，動萬物而不止，不足以喻其效矣。此豈非內外臣工輔理承化者之責哉？《詩》曰：「嗟爾君子，無恒安處。靖共爾位，正直是與。」敢以為今之在位者告。「民之質矣，日用飲食。群黎百姓，徧為爾德。」敢以為太平盛治無疆頌焉。
translation_en:
…or a single act that accords with His Majesty’s wishes, they must diligently encourage it, seeking to exert their strength to the utmost and remain constant from beginning to end. Whenever a single thought or act runs counter to His Majesty’s commands, they must guard against it with trepidation, seeking to arrest it as it first stirs in their hearts and invariably guarding against unrestrained indulgence. They must cause the sovereign’s beneficence to flow down to the people and the people’s sufferings to be communicated upward. They must encourage the scholars of the realm to cultivate their conduct and settle the people of the realm so that they may pursue their livelihoods in peace. Those nearby must be brought into affectionate allegiance, and those far away into submission. Disturbances beyond the borders will require no punitive expedition; the vital forces within the seas will be pure and harmonious, and all will be well ordered. Auspicious signs will concur and favorable portents gather; blessings will follow, while calamities and anomalous events disappear.

Then, as the Book of Changes says, “Words issue from one’s person and extend to the people”; and, as the Guanzi says, “Commands take effect like flowing water.” Thus will the sovereign’s virtue be spread abroad and his beneficence flow abundantly downward. Even the wind, which moves swiftly, penetrates everywhere, and ceaselessly stirs the myriad things, would be inadequate as an analogy for these effects. Is this not the responsibility of officials at court and in the provinces who assist in government and carry forward the sovereign’s transforming influence? The Book of Odes says: “Ah, you gentlemen, do not continually rest at ease. Attend reverently to your offices, associating with the upright.” I venture to offer these words as an admonition to those now holding office. “The people, in their simple nature, daily eat and drink. All the common people everywhere model themselves upon your virtue.” I venture to offer these words as an unending hymn of praise to this flourishing reign of great peace.

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
第二問
金達
同考試官給事中湯批此作能探本于心深
達聖賢奧旨匪徒明經之士矣敬服
同考試官檢討裴批經學本以用世漢儒
以下自失之此作能究其詳取之非特以其博洽也
同考試官侍講邢批得窮經致用之實匪
徒事乎言語文字間者將拭目以待子矣
同考試官侍讀陳批闡明經學殆盡且詞
===
雅氣昌錄此以式多士
考試官侍講學士尹批窮經致用必有本以出之觀
子所述庶幾知所先後矣占其致用之必不謬也
考試官大學士李批經學非明於義理者取舍
鮮有不眩此作敘論精當可以觀所養矣
聖人之作經也固以道而垂萬世之訓君
子之窮經也貴因言而達聖人之心經者
道之寓也心者道之主也道寓於經則窮
經以求聖人之道者所以立致用之本心

translation_en:
Second Question

Jin Da

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Supervising Secretary: “This essay can probe the foundation in the mind and penetrate deeply into the profound meaning of the sages and worthies. Its author is more than merely a scholar versed in the Classics. I admire him respectfully.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Pei, Examining Editor: “Classical learning was originally intended for practical service to the world. From the Han Confucians onward, scholars themselves lost sight of this. This essay thoroughly investigates the matter; its selection is not merely on account of its breadth of learning.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Xing, Expositor-in-Waiting: “You have grasped the substance of thoroughly investigating the Classics and putting that learning into practice, rather than merely occupying yourself with words and writing. I shall watch your future achievements with keen anticipation.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Reader-in-Waiting: “This essay elucidates classical learning almost exhaustively; moreover, its language is elegant and its spirit vigorous. It is included here to serve as a model for the many scholars.”

Comment by Examiner Yin, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: “Thorough investigation of the Classics and the practical application of learning must proceed from a foundation. Judging by what you have written, you seem to understand what comes first and what follows. I predict that your application of learning will assuredly not go astray.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Grand Secretary: “In classical learning, those who lack a clear understanding of moral principles seldom avoid confusion about what to accept and what to reject. This essay’s exposition and argument are precise and apt, revealing the author’s cultivation.”

When the sages composed the Classics, their purpose was assuredly to transmit teachings for all ages through the Way. When the gentleman thoroughly investigates the Classics, what matters is that he reach the minds of the sages through their words. The Classics are where the Way resides; the mind is the master of the Way. Since the Way resides in the Classics, thoroughly investigating the Classics to seek the Way of the sages establishes the foundation for practical application. The mind…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
主乎道則因經而達聖人之心者所以探
會通之原原據則學皆自得經可得而明
矣本立則萬物皆備用可得而利矣不然
則義疏是務而不考諸身心誦說雖勤而
無裨於實用其於聖人之經所昧者多矣
安望其能措之用哉持此而論則漢唐宋
諸儒之窮經可得而推矣夫經非他也天
地之道聖人筆之書以為後世訓者也其
用通于天下而要之不外乎一理其理散
===
于萬事而約之實原於一心易者言乎心
之時也書者言乎心之中也詩者言乎心
之性情也禮者言乎心之節文也春秋者
言乎心之變也故深于易者潔靜精微而
不賊深于書者疏通知遠而不誣深于詩
者溫柔敦厚而不愚深于禮者恭儉莊敬
而不煩深于春秋者屬辭比事而不亂蘊
之為盛德發之為大業窮則其道明達則
其道行而所性無加損焉者也唐虞三代

punctuated: 主乎道，則因經而達聖人之心者，所以探會通之原。原據，則學皆自得，經可得而明矣；本立，則萬物皆備，用可得而利矣。不然，則義疏是務，而不考諸身心；誦說雖勤，而無裨於實用，其於聖人之經所昧者多矣，安望其能措之用哉？持此而論，則漢唐宋諸儒之窮經可得而推矣。夫經非他也，天地之道，聖人筆之書，以為後世訓者也。其用通于天下，而要之不外乎一理；其理散于萬事，而約之實原於一心。《易》者，言乎心之時也；《書》者，言乎心之中也；《詩》者，言乎心之性情也；《禮》者，言乎心之節文也；《春秋》者，言乎心之變也。故深于《易》者，潔靜精微而不賊；深于《書》者，疏通知遠而不誣；深于《詩》者，溫柔敦厚而不愚；深于《禮》者，恭儉莊敬而不煩；深于《春秋》者，屬辭比事而不亂。蘊之為盛德，發之為大業；窮則其道明，達則其道行，而所性無加損焉者也。唐虞三代
translation_en:
…presides over the Way, then reaching the sages’ minds through the Classics is the means of probing the source of comprehensive understanding. Once that source is secured [?], all learning becomes one’s own attainment, and the Classics can be understood. Once the foundation is established, the myriad things are all present within oneself, and practical application can be effective. Otherwise, one devotes oneself to commentaries without testing them against one’s own person and mind. However diligently one recites and expounds, this contributes nothing to practical application. With so much about the sages’ Classics remaining obscure to such a person, how could one expect him to put them into practice? Judged on this basis, the classical scholarship of the Confucians of the Han, Tang, and Song can be assessed.

The Classics are nothing other than the Way of Heaven and Earth, committed to writing by the sages to instruct later generations. Their application extends throughout the world, yet in essence does not go beyond a single principle. That principle is dispersed among the myriad affairs, yet, reduced to its essentials, it truly originates in a single mind. The Changes speaks of the mind’s responsiveness to the times; the Documents, of the mind’s central equilibrium; the Odes, of the mind’s nature and feelings; the Rites, of the mind’s regulated and patterned expression; and the Spring and Autumn Annals, of the mind’s adaptations to change. Thus, those deeply versed in the Changes are pure, tranquil, precise, and subtle without becoming injurious; those deeply versed in the Documents are broadly informed and understand distant matters without becoming unreliable; those deeply versed in the Odes are gentle, kindly, sincere, and generous without becoming foolish; those deeply versed in the Rites are respectful, frugal, dignified, and reverent without becoming burdensome; and those deeply versed in the Spring and Autumn Annals connect statements and compare events without becoming confused. Stored within, this becomes abundant virtue; expressed outwardly, it becomes great achievement. In obscurity, their Way is clear; in prominence, their Way is put into practice. What belongs to their nature undergoes neither increase nor diminution. In the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
其治渾渾爾其俗熈熈爾其民皥皥爾未
有六經而何有窮經之名哉惟夫精一執
中萬世心學之源以啓而其布列于有位
者罔非賢聖之儔是故涵之為經綸之蘊
運之為經國之猷言之為經常之訓筆之
為經世之文不必有經而經由此出也禹
臯稷契伊傅周召隆聲稱著事業卓乎不
可尚已周室既衰王綱弗振孔子以聖德
而厄於季世取六經而刪述之明天文修
===
人紀繼往聖開來學而六經之教始彰戰
國分爭延及秦火漢帝以儒術為重務求
六經而表章之搜遺書興禮樂建學校選
茂材而明經之名始著豈非以聖經之訓
大道攸存而窮經之學固儒者致用之本
哉是故言易自淄川田生言書自濟南伏
生言詩自轅固生韓太傅言禮自魯高堂
生言春秋自胡毋生諸儒更相傳述一時
學士彬彬嚮風而經術盛矣當是時也上

translation_en:
…their government was harmonious and whole, their customs joyful, and their people contented. The Six Classics did not yet exist, so how could there have been any designation for plumbing the Classics? Through refinement and single-mindedness, and holding fast to the mean, the source of the learning of the mind for all ages was opened; those arrayed in office were all companions of worthies and sages. Thus, held within, this learning constituted the accumulated resources for ordering affairs; put into action, it became plans for governing the state; spoken, it became teachings of enduring norms; committed to writing, it became texts for ordering the world. There was no need for preexisting Classics: the Classics emerged from this. Yu, Gao Yao, Ji, Xie, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao won great renown and accomplished illustrious deeds, towering beyond all possibility of being surpassed.

After the house of Zhou declined and royal authority could no longer be upheld, Confucius, possessed of sagely virtue yet beset by adversity in a declining age, took the Six Classics and edited and transmitted them. He elucidated the patterns of Heaven, set human relationships in order, continued the work of earlier sages, and opened the way for future learners. Only then did the teaching of the Six Classics become manifest. The divisions and conflicts of the Warring States continued down to the Qin burning of the books. The Han emperors esteemed Confucian learning, diligently sought out the Six Classics and brought them to prominence, collected surviving writings, revived rites and music, established schools, and selected men of outstanding talent. Only then did the designation “mastery of the Classics” become prominent. Was this not because the teachings of the sagely Classics were where the Great Way resided, and because the study that plumbs the Classics is indeed the foundation upon which Confucian scholars put their learning into practice?

Thus, the exposition of the Book of Changes derived from Master Tian of Zichuan; that of the Book of Documents from Master Fu of Jinan; that of the Book of Odes from Master Yuan Gu and Grand Preceptor Han; that of the Rites from Master Gaotang of Lu; and that of the Spring and Autumn Annals from Master Huwu. The various Confucian scholars transmitted and expounded these teachings in succession. The scholars of the age, accomplished and refined, followed their example, and classical learning flourished. At that time, the ruler…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
崇教化士志文學人有師授業有專門其
討論之力能明聖經於既晦之餘宜其致
用之迹必能達聖經於躬行之顯也柰何
漢儒之學雖有師承之授而出口入耳殊
乏體驗之功是以窮經之名雖盛而其實
則微矣探索雖專而穿鑿附會失則為誣
章句徒詳而詭異滅裂失則為罔慕功名
者曲學阿世其彼善於此者則又執已見
以自私如是而語窮經者末矣故學雖不
===
同其無裨於用則均也如卦氣直日京房
精於占候之數矣然身犯恭顯之變而不
能自保其於易之占候何如也說詩解頤
匡衡能明關雎之義矣然身任元成之傅
而阿附取容其於詩之事君何如也夏侯
勝得洪範之旨而青紫拾芥之說則所志
者卑矣董仲舒達天人之際而縱陽閉陰
之論則流於迂且誕矣之數子者皆漢儒
巨擘尚有遺議下此者又奚足論哉經術

punctuated: 崇教化，士志文學，人有師授，業有專門。其討論之力，能明聖經於既晦之餘，宜其致用之迹，必能達聖經於躬行之顯也。柰何漢儒之學，雖有師承之授，而出口入耳，殊乏體驗之功。是以窮經之名雖盛，而其實則微矣。探索雖專，而穿鑿附會，失則為誣；章句徒詳，而詭異滅裂，失則為罔。慕功名者，曲學阿世；其彼善於此者，則又執已見以自私。如是而語窮經者，末矣。故學雖不同，其無裨於用則均也。如卦氣直日，京房精於占候之數矣，然身犯恭顯之變，而不能自保，其於易之占候何如也？說詩解頤，匡衡能明關雎之義矣，然身任元成之傅，而阿附取容，其於詩之事君何如也？夏侯勝得洪範之旨，而青紫拾芥之說，則所志者卑矣。董仲舒達天人之際，而縱陽閉陰之論，則流於迂且誕矣。之數子者，皆漢儒巨擘，尚有遺議，下此者又奚足論哉？經術
translation_en:
…promoted moral transformation, while scholars devoted themselves to literary learning. Each person received instruction from a teacher, and each field had its specialist tradition. Their efforts in discussion and inquiry could illuminate the sages’ classics after these had fallen into obscurity; one would therefore expect their practical achievements to give those classics manifest expression in personal conduct. Yet why was it that, although Han scholars received learning transmitted through teachers, it merely passed from mouth to ear, with so little effort devoted to understanding it through personal experience? Thus, although their reputation for thoroughly investigating the classics flourished, the substance was slight. Their inquiries were specialized, but strained interpretations and forced connections led them into misrepresentation; their analyses of chapters and sentences were merely elaborate, while bizarre interpretations and careless fragmentation led them into deception. Those who coveted achievement and fame distorted learning to flatter the age; even those somewhat better than these clung to their own views for private ends. To speak of thoroughly investigating the classics in this fashion was to attend only to its peripheral aspects. Hence, although their learning differed, they were alike in contributing nothing to practical use.

Take the assignment of hexagram qi to particular days: Jing Fang was expert in the numerical methods of prognostication. Yet he became embroiled in the upheaval involving Hong Gong and Shi Xian and could not protect himself. What, then, had he gained from the prognosticatory teachings of the Book of Changes? Kuang Heng’s explanations of the Book of Odes brought smiles of delight, and he could elucidate the meaning of “Guanju” (“The Ospreys”). Yet, serving as tutor to Emperors Yuan and Cheng, he ingratiated himself through flattery. What, then, had he gained from the Book of Odes’ teachings on serving one’s ruler? Xiahou Sheng grasped the purport of “The Great Plan,” but his claim that obtaining the blue and purple insignia of high office was like picking up a straw revealed the baseness of his aspirations. Dong Zhongshu understood the relationship between Heaven and humanity, but his theory of releasing yang and shutting off yin strayed into the impractical and preposterous. These several men [?] were all leading figures among Han scholars, yet even they remained open to criticism. How could those beneath them be worth discussing? Classical learning…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
所以經世而儒者不能以心求之則輔理
承化之功未有外心而能致者矣漢儒窮
經而不能以致用非經不足以適用所用
者非其經也非窮之力有未盡所以窮之
者未探其本也自漢而降心學愈荒而六
經之道益晦矣唐雖以經術取士然溺於
詞章習於聲偶所謂經義者徒筌蹄耳而
況孔穎達之正義多雜讖緯之說陸長源
之春秋傳無救穿鑿之失尚何以經術為
===
哉文人附會其弊愈滋無惑乎經學之遠
不逮漢也及宋文運復興道學丕振真儒
輩出求不傳之緒而續之易傳作於程子
本義作於朱子而陰陽之奧以明書傳註
於蔡沈而政事之典以彰春秋傳註於胡
安國而名分之辨以詳至若詩經集傳儀
禮集解則朱子作之自謂於世有補可無
遺憾而六經之道如日中天矣盖其學以
道德性命為本而不失之虛以身心體驗

punctuated:
所以經世，而儒者不能以心求之，則輔理承化之功，未有外心而能致者矣。漢儒窮經而不能以致用，非經不足以適用，所用者非其經也；非窮之力有未盡，所以窮之者未探其本也。自漢而降，心學愈荒，而六經之道益晦矣。唐雖以經術取士，然溺於詞章，習於聲偶，所謂經義者徒筌蹄耳。而況孔穎達之《正義》多雜讖緯之說，陸長源之《春秋傳》無救穿鑿之失，尚何以經術為哉？文人附會，其弊愈滋，無惑乎經學之遠不逮漢也。
及宋，文運復興，道學丕振，真儒輩出，求不傳之緒而續之。《易傳》作於程子，《本義》作於朱子，而陰陽之奧以明；《書傳》註於蔡沈，而政事之典以彰；《春秋傳》註於胡安國，而名分之辨以詳。至若《詩經集傳》、《儀禮集解》，則朱子作之，自謂於世有補，可無遺憾，而六經之道如日中天矣。盖其學以道德性命為本，而不失之虛；以身心體驗
translation_en:
…is the means by which the world is ordered. Yet if scholars cannot seek it through the mind, then the achievement of assisting governance and carrying forward moral transformation can never be attained apart from the mind. The Han scholars investigated the classics exhaustively but could not put them to practical use. This was not because the classics were inadequate for practical application, but because what they applied was not the teaching of those classics. Nor was it because their efforts at investigation were insufficient; rather, their manner of investigation failed to probe the root. From the Han onward, the learning of the mind fell increasingly into neglect, and the Way of the Six Classics grew ever more obscure. Although the Tang selected officials through classical learning, scholars immersed themselves in literary composition and became habituated to tonal patterns and parallel phrasing. What they called the meaning of the classics was merely a fish trap or rabbit snare—the means without the end. Moreover, Kong Yingda’s Correct Meaning mingled in many doctrines of prophecy and apocrypha, while Lu Changyuan’s Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals [?] failed to remedy the faults of forced interpretation. How could this still count as classical learning? Men of letters contrived strained connections, and these abuses multiplied. It is no wonder that classical scholarship fell far short of that of the Han.
With the Song, literary culture revived and the learning of the Way flourished greatly. True Confucian scholars emerged in succession, seeking out and renewing the broken thread of transmission. Master Cheng composed the Commentary on the Changes, and Master Zhu composed the Original Meaning, thereby illuminating the mysteries of yin and yang. Cai Shen composed the Commentary on the Documents, thereby making manifest the canons of government. Hu Anguo composed the Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, thereby clarifying distinctions of status and duty. As for the Collected Commentaries on the Classic of Poetry and the Collected Explanations of the Ceremonies and Rites [?], Master Zhu composed them, himself saying that they benefited the world and that he could have no remaining regrets. Thus the Way of the Six Classics shone like the sun at its zenith. Their learning took the Way, virtue, human nature, and Heaven’s mandate as its foundation, without lapsing into emptiness; it took personal experience through body and mind…

title: 嘉靖三十五年會試錄
text:
為實而不流於罔以格物窮理為要而不
病於荒是以道與心一經與道會而自得
之學信非漢後諸儒所可同日語者也宋
儒經術之盛如此而事功之顯竟不躋古
三代之隆此又誰之過哉或隱而未見於
用或用而未竟其施時勢限之而於經固
無病也雖然通古今而無弊者理曠百世
而相感者心唐虞三代之士心即經也故
經垂而用弘宋儒以心求經者也故經明
===
而道顯漢之訓詁唐之詞章風斯下矣用
斯窒矣學者欲以致用其窮經宜何如哉
求吾心之神化則得易之變由是而與時
偕行變易從道皆易之施也求吾心之紀
綱則盡書之事而察於物類明于治體皆
書之用也求吾心之性情則達詩之義由
是而事理通達心氣和平皆詩之發也求
吾心之序則得禮之本由是以昭天常以
立人紀皆禮之形也求吾心之權衡則得

Thus the Way and the mind became one, and the Classics accorded with the Way. Their learning, attained through personal understanding, truly cannot be spoken of in the same breath as that of the scholars after the Han. The Song scholars’ mastery of the Classics flourished to this extent, yet their manifest achievements in government never reached the heights of the ancient Three Dynasties. Whose fault was this? Some remained in retirement and never put their learning into practice; others entered service but did not complete its implementation. The circumstances of their times constrained them: there was certainly no fault in the Classics. Nevertheless, principle runs through antiquity and the present without failing, and minds resonate with one another across a hundred generations. For the scholars of the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, the mind itself was the Classics; hence the Classics were handed down and their application was far-reaching. The Song scholars sought the Classics through the mind; hence the Classics became clear and the Way was revealed. …yet scholars of the age themselves fall into these failings without realizing it. This essay repeatedly weighs and adjudicates the issues and has a firm, considered position. It is selected to serve as a model for scholars who pursue breadth of learning.

Examiner Yin, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: Confucian scholars need not reject the writings of the Hundred Schools. It is enough to judge and select according to the Way, without becoming immersed in their errors. This essay grasps that principle.

Examiner Li, Grand Secretary, comments: It distinguishes and refutes erroneous and unfounded views, and its judgments and selections clearly rest on a firm, considered position. It does more than echo the ancients and merits inclusion.

In learning, the gentleman seeks breadth, leaving nothing unexamined; in seeking essentials, he wishes to reach the ultimate point toward which learning leads. Drawing broadly serves to widen the scope of his interests and extend the beginnings of his knowledge; bringing these back to essentials serves to return to their source and bring his learning to substantive fruition. Thus, regarding the writings of the Hundred Schools, the gentleman simply keeps them: there is no need to reject them. He simply selects from them: he must not proceed without bounds or discrimination. You, honored examiners, have posed a policy question to the candidates concerning the various masters, wishing to see arguments that weigh and adjudicate their views. Presumably you intend to guide students so that they are not confused about which direction to follow. This is a most generous intention. Dare I offer no words in reply?

At the height of the Three Dynasties, the Way prevailed above and instruction was clear below. Scholars devoted themselves to personal practice as the basis of learning; they did not stray and become immersed in writings contrary to the sages. Once the Great Way became obscured, learning lost its authoritative lineage. Scholars who grasped only one aspect each pursued what they wished, making it a method of their own; thus the arts of the Way were fragmented throughout the world. The extravagant proliferation of the various masters’ teachings therefore arose entirely from the obstruction of sagely learning. Nevertheless, …

…Their writings range freely over the transformations of past and present and elucidate the true circumstances of things and affairs. Their intelligence suffices to exhaust the subtleties, and their thought to comprehend the essentials; each stands independently as a school in its own right. Thus the gentleman still sometimes draws upon them. If one thoroughly examines the reasons for their similarities and differences and judges them against the sages, investigates their divergent intentions and brings them within the compass of principle, how could they go so far as to become a departure from our Way? Thus the teachings of the various masters are not something the widely learned discard.

The rulers of the Han, distressed by the devastation of the Qin book burning, gathered scattered and lost writings and opened channels for the presentation of books, thereby collecting the surviving writings of the realm. The Six Arts were established in the official schools, and the writings of the Hundred Schools filled the imperial library. Only then could those works that had narrowly escaped destruction be consulted as evidence. Liu Xiang collated texts in the Tianlu Pavilion and set out their general contents; Liu Xin brought the collected books together and submitted a synopsis. In composing the History of the Han, Ban Gu in turn drew on that synopsis, abridging it to its essentials and comprehensively recording the texts in the bibliographical treatise, “Arts and Writings.” Only then could the scattered and disparate writings be systematically recorded.

Thus, speaking of the ten schools: the Confucians record the cycles of cosmic forces [?]; the Legalists, laws and institutions; the School of Names, names and realities; the Mohists, strengthening the fundamental occupation and economizing on expenditure; the Diplomatists, disputation and deception; the Eclectics, diverse doctrines; the Agriculturalists, sowing and cultivation; and the School of Minor Sayings, rustic utterances and popular disputes [?].
